reasoning: Case sensitivity and identifier boundaries interact: case-insensitive matching over-collects. Plain substring matching inside camelCase identifiers ignores naming style. The right query respects the language's identifier structure rather than tuning a single flag. Deciding case behaviour is a semantic choice about what counts as the same name.
answer: Search per identifier form deliberately: 'rg -n "\bLogger\b" src' for the exact token, 'rg -n "(create|get)Logger\b"' for factories, and a case-sensitive variant when casing distinguishes types from instances. Use 'rg -S' or explicit alternation for camelCase variants rather than blanket -i, which also matches prose and comments. Verify by checking a few files for the expected definitions and by confirming comment-only hits were excluded with '-g "!*.md"'.

instruction: You must decide which files to read first out of 200 search hits. Explain how a search tool's counting output changes the reading order and why that ordering is defensible.
reasoning: Reading hits in file order spends effort on incidental matches, while density of matches per file is a cheap proxy for centrality. Grouping and ranking turns an unreadable list into a plan. The ranking is still a heuristic, so it guides reading rather than replacing it.
answer: Produce per-file counts with 'rg -c "pattern" src | sort -t: -k2 -rn | head -20' and start with the highest-density files, then confirm each is relevant by opening it. Restrict by extension, for example '-g "*.ts"', to drop tests and docs first, and use 'git grep -c' when generated output is committed. Verify the ordering by noting whether the top hits are definitions or call sites, since a file with one definition and many references is more central than a file with many mentions in comments.

instruction: You need to know whether a string existed in the release tag 'v2.4.0' rather than in your branch. Explain the search form and what it lets you conclude about when the string appeared.
reasoning: A revision-scoped search reads the tree as it was, so absence at that tag is evidence about that snapshot rather than about history. Combining it with pickaxe search turns a presence check into a dating check. The distinction matters when deciding whether a bug is a regression or pre-existing.
answer: Search the tag directly: 'git grep -n "deprecatedFlag" v2.4.0' and compare with the same search on HEAD. Then date the change with 'git log -S "deprecatedFlag" --oneline v2.4.0..HEAD' to see additions after the tag, and 'git log -S ... v2.4.0' for what preceded it. Verify by opening the candidate commit's diff to confirm the string was introduced rather than merely moved, since a rename can change occurrence counts.

instruction: You must find every file that both references 'feature/flags' and does not already import the new provider. Explain the search construction and why two sequential searches can mislead.
reasoning: Set difference between two hit lists answers a structural question that a single regex handles poorly, but it depends on normalising both lists to the same path form. Differences in relative paths or file ordering produce phantom entries. The method is sound only if the comparison is apples to apples.
answer: Build both sets and subtract: 'comm -23 <(git grep -l "feature/flags" | sort) <(git grep -l "FlagsProvider" | sort)'. Ensure both commands run from the same directory so paths match, and use 'sort' on both inputs because comm requires sorted data. Verify by grepping a sample of the output for both patterns, since an import may be written through a barrel file that the second search does not name.

instruction: You need the CSS rules for a class used in JSX but styled in a design-system package inside node_modules. Explain how to search installed dependencies without pulling in the whole tree.
reasoning: Dependency sources are the only place generated or vendored styles exist, and searching all of node_modules is slow and noisy. Bounding the search by package and file type makes it tractable. Reaching into dependencies for reading is legitimate; editing them is not.
answer: Scope the search: 'rg -n "\.card-title" node_modules/@acme/design-system/dist' or 'rg --files-with-matches -g "*.css" "card-title" node_modules/@acme/design-system', and use '--max-depth' plus a package-name glob to avoid scanning unrelated trees. Confirm the class is not overridden by your own stylesheet with a second search in src. Verify the conclusion by inspecting the specificity and source order in the built CSS rather than the package source, since bundling can reorder output.

instruction: An environment variable 'FEATURE_BILLING_URL' seems set but the app reads a different value. Describe the search that finds every place this variable is named, including configuration outside source files.
reasoning: Configuration lives across dotfiles, manifests, CI definitions and infrastructure code, each of which a source-only search misses. Searching only code produces a confident but incomplete answer. Broadening by file type is what reveals the conflicting definition.
answer: Search all tracked files regardless of extension, for example 'git grep -n "FEATURE_BILLING_URL"', which includes YAML, Dockerfiles, Makefiles and shell scripts, then add untracked and ignored files with 'rg -u --hidden -g "!.git" FEATURE_BILLING_URL'. Include .env files deliberately because they are usually ignored by default. Verify by listing every definition found and comparing against the value the process actually has, read from inside the runtime.

instruction: You need to know which dependency calls a deprecated method. Explain how searching inside node_modules differs from searching the repository and what the result cannot tell you.
reasoning: The dependency tree is the right corpus, but searching it requires excluding maps and bundled artifacts to get meaningful hits. Knowing which package calls a method still leaves the question of whether the version constraint can be raised. Search results identify a caller, not a remedy.
answer: Search installed packages while skipping noise: 'rg -n "legacyMethod" node_modules -g "!*.map" -g "!*.min.js" -g "!**/dist/**/*.d.ts"', then identify the owning package from the path with 'rg -l' and read its package.json to see the version. Cross-check the upstream repository's issue tracker or changelog for a replacement, and use 'npm ls <pkg>' to see whether you depend on it directly or transitively. Verify by confirming the call site is in shipped code rather than a test directory inside the package.

instruction: A TODO comment names a person but git log has been squashed. Explain how to attribute the line and what uncertainty remains after attribution.
reasoning: Blame attributes the commit that last touched the line, which after a squash is the squashed commit rather than the original author. It answers who wrote the current text, not who owns the intent. Naming a person in a comment is documentation, not a responsibility record.
answer: Run 'git blame -L <start>,<end> path/to/file' to find the commit that introduced the line and read its message and author, then confirm the comment itself with 'git log -1 --format="%an %ae" <sha>'. Because a squash collapses real history, the earliest surviving commit may predate the actual decision. Verify by cross-checking the linked issue or pull request referenced in the message, and treat the person named in the comment as a hint rather than an owner.

instruction: You must find every file that hardcodes the string 'http://' where HTTPS should be used, excluding tests, fixtures and documentation examples. Write the search and explain the exclusion decision.
reasoning: A raw pattern matches prose, mocks and negative test cases, which inflates the result and invites unnecessary edits. Excluding by path and file type is a judgment about intent, so it must be justified and then spot-checked. Over-exclusion silently drops real issues.
answer: Use a scoped search with explicit exclusions, for example 'rg -n "http://" src -g "!*test*" -g "!*fixture*" -g "!*.md"', and include tracked configuration with 'git grep -n "http://" -- ":(exclude)*.md"'. Verify the exclusions by listing files they removed and reviewing the list once, so a source file with a bad default is not dropped. Then read each remaining hit to distinguish a redirect rule, which legitimately uses http, from an insecure client URL.

instruction: Searching for the port number 3000 returns 400 matches across the repository. Explain how to make this search meaningful and what makes numeric search unreliable.
reasoning: A short number matches unrelated values, array indices, timeouts and version fragments, so recall is high and precision is near zero. Meaning requires co-locating the number with an adjacent concept. Numeric literals are the worst search key in a codebase.
answer: Anchor the number to context: 'rg -n "(PORT|port)\D{0,3}3000"' or search with surrounding syntax such as '"3000"|:3000|localhost:3000', and restrict to configuration-like files with '-g "*.{env,json,yaml,yml,toml,js,ts}"'. Enumerate the mechanisms that can set a port, including an environment default, and check the server's listen call to see which source wins. Verify by printing the effective port from the running process rather than trusting any file.

instruction: You need every place an error message literal is produced so you can localize it, but the string appears only once in the source and twice in the UI. Explain the search strategy that resolves the discrepancy.
reasoning: Text shown to users may be assembled from fragments, templated, or come from a dependency, so the exact literal need not exist in source. The absence of a match is evidence about how the message is produced, not about whether it exists. Widening the query is the correct next step.
answer: Search on a distinctive substring rather than the full sentence, for example 'rg -n "payment method declined" -i' and then 'rg -n "declined" src', allowing for concatenation and interpolation. Check for a message catalog or translation file, and search node_modules in case the string comes from a library or validator. Verify by finding the throw site, confirming it is reachable from the failing request, and checking whether tests assert the full sentence.

instruction: You must find all definitions of a GraphQL field across resolvers, type definitions and generated files. Explain how to structure the search so generated content does not dominate and how to avoid missing hand-written resolvers.
reasoning: Generated schema and type files contain many exact matches that no one edits, so including them obscures the authored definitions. Excluding them by path is safe only if the exclusion is verified. Two different search scopes answer two different questions and should both be run.
answer: Run two searches: one over generated or type definition files to enumerate the contract, and one over source excluding generated paths, for example 'rg -n "myField" src -g "!**/generated/**"'. Identify generated files by headers or by build configuration, since a path heuristic alone can be wrong. For resolvers, search the field name as a key, for example '"myField"' or 'myField:', and check for a resolver map. Verify by listing every declared field in the served schema from a query rather than only from files.

instruction: You need to search the content of a .wasm or other binary artifact for a symbol name. Explain the tool that makes this possible and how to interpret an absence of results.
reasoning: Text search on binary files often refuses or reports only that the file matched, so extracting printable runs is the practical approach. Absence is weak evidence, because names can be minified or encoded differently than expected. The interpretation must account for what the tool can see.
answer: Use 'strings artifact.wasm | grep -i "symbolName"' to dump printable sequences, and 'strings -n 8 -t x' if you need offsets for correlation. Confirm the artifact is the expected one by comparing its hash with the build output, since a stale copy produces false negatives. Treat absence as inconclusive rather than proof: the name may have been stripped. Verify by searching for a literal that must survive, such as an error message, and if it is also absent, conclude the file or the search assumption is wrong.

instruction: You must find every file in a monorepo that imports a module you are about to delete, including files in packages that are not checked out in the current workspace. Explain how to search without switching branches or updating each package.
reasoning: A monorepo's dependency edges cross package boundaries, so a scoped search in one package under-reports. Searching the whole repository from the root is cheap, while searching staled or unlinked packages requires repository-level tools. Under-counting references is how deletions break CI.
answer: From the repository root run 'git grep -n "oldModule" -- "*.ts" "*.tsx"', which covers every tracked file across packages, and follow with 'rg -n "from .[\x27\"](@scope/pkg|\.\./)oldModule"' for specifier forms. Also search alias forms declared in each package's tsconfig paths, since an alias hides the path. Verify by deleting on a branch and running the workspace-wide build, because the search cannot see dynamic or computed imports.

instruction: You want to find unused exports. Explain why a search for the export name is only the first stage and what additional evidence is needed before removing anything.
reasoning: Absence of a textual reference does not establish dead code, because exports may be consumed through barrel re-exports, dynamic access, type-only imports, or by external packages. Removing code on the basis of one search is a guess presented as cleanup. Multiple independent checks reduce the risk.
answer: Start with 'git grep -n "symbolName"' across the repository, then check barrel files that re-export it, dynamic access patterns such as bracket notation, and whether the package publishes it, which you can confirm in 'exports' or the public type surface. A tool that understands modules, or the compiler with noUnusedLocals, gives stronger evidence than search. Verify by deleting the export on a branch and running the build, tests and type check together, since a passing type check alone may not cover the entry point.

instruction: You need to know whether a route path exists in the shipped bundle when the source maps are unavailable and the code is minified. Explain how search works on that artifact and what conclusion it supports.
reasoning: Minification renames identifiers but preserves string literals, which is why a URL path can still be searched in a bundle. Matching on a variable name is invalid for the same reason. Choosing the right kind of token makes the artifact searchable.
answer: Search stable literals rather than identifiers: 'curl -s https://cdn/app/main.hash.js | rg -o "/api/orders/[a-z]+" | sort -u', and grep for error strings and template fragments that survive minification. To confirm a handler exists, look for its literal message or its registration pattern. Verify by requesting the route directly and reading the status, since presence in a bundle proves the code was included, not that it is reachable at runtime.

instruction: You must confirm whether a dependency inside a distributed image layer still contains a vulnerable call. Explain how to search the artifact without extracting the whole image to disk.
reasoning: A published artifact is the ground truth for what ships, and searching its layers is legitimate inspection, but extracting gigabytes to grep one string is wasteful. Streaming and selective extraction keep the check cheap. The image content, not the repository, answers what was deployed.
answer: Inspect layer metadata and stream content: list layers with 'docker history --no-trunc <image>', then run the search inside a container without persisting it, for example 'docker run --rm --entrypoint sh <image> -c "grep -rn vulnerableMethod node_modules/pkg/dist | head"', or 'docker create' plus 'docker cp' of only the target path. Verify by comparing the file's checksum inside the image with the package version you expected, since a stale base layer may hold an older copy than the manifest claims.

instruction: You want every 'try' block that calls an async function but never awaits it. Explain why a single grep cannot answer this and what combination of tools can.
reasoning: The condition spans block structure and semantics, which line matching cannot model, and negation within a region is outside regex's reliable reach. Text search can narrow candidates, while a static analysis rule can assert the pattern. Reporting a grep count as the answer would be false precision.
answer: Use search to narrow and analysis to decide: start with 'rg -n "await" src' to find async usage and compare against 'rg -l "\.then\(|async " src', then express the real rule with a lint rule such as require-await or no-floating-promises, or a semgrep or ast-grep query over the AST. Run the linter with the rule enabled to get precise locations. Verify by inspecting a few reported files to confirm the rule matches your intent rather than trusting the count.

instruction: A stack trace names a line in a file you have never opened. Explain how to use search context flags to read enough of the code to form a hypothesis, and why a match-only output is insufficient.
reasoning: A single matching line omits the surrounding logic that determines whether the reported value could even occur, so a hit without context invites a wrong causal story. Deliberately pulling surrounding lines converts a location into evidence. The choice of context size is part of the reasoning.
answer: Retrieve the region rather than the line: 'rg -n -C 25 "throw new ValidationError" src', or view the exact area with 'sed -n "120,170p" file'. For a repository-wide read, 'git grep -n -B3 -A6 pattern'. Also open the enclosing function so you can see guards and early returns, since the trace line is only where failure surfaced. Verify by forming a falsifiable prediction, for example a specific input value reaching the throw, and testing it directly.

instruction: Before making a branch public you must check the repository for committed secrets, including in history. Explain which tool answers this and why searching current files is inadequate.
reasoning: Secrets remain retrievable in history even after deletion, so a working-tree scan gives false assurance. Dedicated scanners look for high-entropy strings across revisions, which a keyword grep will not find. The scope of the scan determines whether the conclusion is trustworthy.
answer: Run a history-aware secret scanner such as 'gitleaks detect --source .' or 'trufflehog filesystem .', which examine revisions rather than only the checkout, and confirm the target branch's history is fully fetched, since a shallow clone hides commits. Then inspect any finding to determine whether it is a real credential or a fixture. Verify by re-running after any removal, noting that deleting the file does not remove history; that needs history rewriting plus credential rotation, which must be a human-approved decision.

instruction: You need to search files that exist only in your working tree and are ignored, because a generated manifest was accidentally edited. Explain how to include ignored content and the risk of acting on such a file.
reasoning: Default search behaviour hides ignored files, which is usually desirable but silently omits exactly the generated artifacts an agent might have hand-edited. Knowing the override flag turns a false negative into a finding. Editing ignored, generated content has no durable effect, which is a conclusion, not an observation.
answer: Search with ignored files included, for example 'rg -uu "generatedAt" .' or explicitly target the path, then check whether it is ignored with 'git check-ignore -v path/to/file' and whether a generator produces it. Confirm the generator's configuration to see what value it would write instead. Verify by re-running the generator and checking whether your edit disappears, which proves the file is derived; if it does not, the manifest is hand-maintained and the fix belongs there.

instruction: You must inventory every route in an Express application where routers are mounted in several files. Explain why a text search for route strings will undercount and what to combine with it.
reasoning: Path prefixes are composed at mount time, so the full URL exists nowhere as a literal. Text search finds fragments, which produces a plausible but incomplete inventory. Enumerating the runtime's own view closes the gap that static search leaves.
answer: Search for the registration calls, 'rg -n "router\.(get|post|put|delete)|app\.use" src', and follow each mount to compose prefixes by reading the nesting. Then produce ground truth from the running app by printing the registered layer paths, or by requesting candidate URLs and reading status codes. Verify by reconciling the two lists and investigating any runtime route the search missed, which indicates a dynamic mount.

instruction: The same user-facing error text appears in four files. Explain how to detect such duplicated literals across a codebase and what a match list does not tell you.
reasoning: Duplicate strings signal either an intentional constant or copy-paste drift, and only the second is a problem. Finding the text is easy; deciding whether it should be centralised requires knowing which sites are reachable from which flows. Search output is a candidate list, not a verdict.
answer: Find repeated literals with a normalised extraction: 'rg -o -N "\x27[^"]{20,}\x27" src | sort | uniq -cd | sort -rn | head', which surfaces strings occurring more than once, or compare error-message constants against a messages module. Then check reachability: which module exports the constant and which files import it. Verify by reading each site's control flow before proposing consolidation, because two identical messages with different remediation instructions should not be merged.

instruction: A teammate says the fix they need is in their stash but they cannot find it with grep. Explain how to search stash content and how to confirm which stash entry they mean.
reasoning: Stash entries live outside the working tree, so ordinary search never sees them, yet they are indexed objects and git can list them. Entries are named by position, which changes as stashes are added and removed, so identification must come from metadata rather than an index. Positional references are a real hazard for destructive commands.
answer: List and inspect: 'git stash list' then 'git stash show -p stash@{0}' for the diff, or search text across stashes with 'git log -g --grep="retry"' and 'git grep -n "pattern" $(git rev-list -g --all 2>/dev/null | head)'. Confirm the entry by its message and date, since stash@{0} is only the most recent and shifts if someone else stashes. Verify by applying to a scratch branch with 'git stash branch <name> stash@{0}' rather than popping in place, so nothing is lost if the content is wrong.

instruction: A file is named by content hash in the build output and you must find its source. Explain the search approach that uses the hash and what additional evidence confirms the mapping.
reasoning: Content-hashed names are deliberately unrelated to source paths, so name search cannot help and the relationship is held by a manifest or by the emitted file itself. Reconstructing the mapping needs the build's metadata, not a guess from filenames. Treating a hash as searchable text yields confident wrong answers.
answer: Look up the hash in the build's own record: check the emitted manifest, asset or stats JSON that pairs logical entry points with hashed filenames, and search the build output directory for a mapping file. Some bundlers can emit a machine-readable manifest, which is the reliable source. Verify by comparing the hash of the candidate source's compiled output with the filename, for example recomputing with the same hashing step, or by requesting the URL and inspecting content-type and body.

instruction: You need counts of a pattern per package in a monorepo with 30 packages. Compare a loop over packages with a single search from the root, and justify your choice.
reasoning: A loop spawns a process per package, which is slower and can produce inconsistent scopes if each run has different ignore rules, while one traversal guarantees a uniform corpus. Uniformity matters as much as speed when the numbers will be compared. The comparison is about measurement validity.
answer: Run one search and group the output: 'rg -c "pattern" . | awk -F/ "{print \$2}" | sort | uniq -c', which keeps the scope consistent, then sort to rank. A loop with 'git grep' per package is acceptable only if you verify each invocation used the same pathspec and revisions. Verify by comparing the sum of per-package counts with a total count from the root, since a mismatch means paths were double-counted or excluded.

instruction: 'rg "TODO"' returns almost nothing in a repository you know contains many TODOs. Explain the two most likely causes and how to test each without guessing.
reasoning: A search tool's defaults exclude hidden and ignored files and may respect a config file that sets additional exclusions. So under-reporting is often a scoping effect rather than an absence of matches. Distinguishing those causes is trivial with a widened search. Accepting an empty result as truth is the actual failure.
answer: Widen deliberately and compare: 'rg -uu --hidden "TODO" .' includes ignored and hidden files, and a difference in counts points to ignore rules or file-type filters. Check for a ripgrep configuration file or RG_FLAGS environment variable that adds exclusions, and confirm with 'rg --files | head' whether expected files are in scope at all. Verify by running a second tool, 'git grep -c TODO', and reconciling any remaining difference with the ignore configuration.

instruction: The functionality you are looking for lives in a git submodule that is not initialised in this checkout. Explain how to search it and what to be careful about when editing there.
reasoning: An uninitialised submodule directory is empty, so a repository-wide search silently omits an entire codebase, producing a confident wrong conclusion. Submodules also belong to a different repository with its own history and review flow. Recognising the boundary changes both search and the safety of editing.
answer: Check submodule state with 'git submodule status' and initialise with 'git submodule update --init --recursive' before searching, then search inside it explicitly since ignore rules often exclude submodule paths. Confirm you are searching the intended revision, because a submodule pins a commit. Any fix belongs in the submodule's own repository, requiring a separate commit and a pointer update here; verify the pinned commit with 'git ls-tree HEAD <path>'.

instruction: You want to know which files were changed by a pull request and whether any of them still reference a symbol you plan to remove. Explain the search scope you would use.
reasoning: Searching the whole repository answers a different question than reviewing a change, and it drowns the relevant hits in unrelated ones. Restricting to the diff's file list aligns evidence with the change under review. The right corpus for a search is a decision, not a default.
answer: Get the changed paths from the diff range, for example 'git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD', then search only those files: 'git grep -n "symbolName" HEAD -- $(git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD)'. Include additions and deletions separately by reading the patch, since a removed reference elsewhere may be outside the diff. Verify by running the project's type check on the branch, because a scoped search cannot see dynamic references or files added after your listing.

instruction: You must find every hardcoded host or protocol value before moving a service to a new domain. Explain why a search for the current hostname is not sufficient coverage.
reasoning: Hostnames also appear in generated configuration, seeds, fixtures, documentation. In values assembled from parts, so an exact-string search returns a list that looks complete and is not. Enumeration must include patterns rather than one literal. Under-reporting here causes production outages.
answer: Search for the shape as well as the literal: 'rg -n "https?://[a-z0-9.-]+" -o src infrastructure | sort -u' to enumerate every URL and then cluster by host, plus targeted searches for the host in configuration files, CI definitions, migration seeds and test fixtures, using 'git grep -n "old\.example\.com"' for tracked content. Also look for split values where the host is concatenated. Verify by checking the running configuration's resolved URLs rather than only the source, since defaults can come from the environment.

instruction: A value is defined in three places and the last one wins, but you cannot tell which. Explain how to trace configuration precedence with search and reading, and why finding all definitions is only half the answer.
reasoning: Precedence is decided by load order and merge semantics in code, not by which definition looks most specific. Locating every definition is necessary but insufficient, since the outcome depends on which assignment executes last. The reasoning step is reading the loader, not counting matches.
answer: Enumerate definitions with 'git grep -n "themeColor"', then read the loading code to see the merge order, for example defaults then file then environment then query parameter, and note whether later sources overwrite or deep-merge. Confirm empirically by setting distinct sentinel values in each source and observing which one the running app reports. Verify by removing one source at a time and re-checking, which proves precedence rather than assuming it from the file you found first.

instruction: You must find where a database column was renamed. Explain how to search migration files as well as code, and what the absence of a migration for a rename implies.
reasoning: Schema changes live in migration history while the application's expectation lives in schema definitions and queries, and a rename can be split across both. If the column exists in the database but no migration renames it, someone changed the database directly. The gap between history and state is the finding.
answer: Search migrations for the old and new names, 'rg -n "(customer_id|clientId)" migrations db', and read the schema definition file and its snapshot to see which name is declared. Then compare with the live database, for example '\d tablename' in psql, to see what actually exists. Verify by checking the migration ledger table for applied versions: a state that no migration can produce indicates manual drift, which must be reconciled with a new migration rather than by editing history.

instruction: The code you are looking for may live in one of six sibling repositories. Explain how to search across them without cloning each one, and the limitation of that approach.
reasoning: Hosted code search spans repositories that are not present locally, which is the right tool for discovery, but it indexes only default branches and skips ignored or generated files. Using it for a survey and a local search for precision separates discovery from verification. Treating an empty hosted search as proof of absence is a common error.
answer: Use the forge's code search, for example 'gh search code "reconcileInventory" --owner acme', to identify which repositories contain the symbol, then clone or fetch only the relevant one for a precise local search with 'git grep'. Confirm the default branch you searched and whether forks are included. Verify locally, since hosted indexes lag pushes and omit ignored files, so an empty result there means 'not indexed', not 'not present'.

instruction: A dependency version appears as '4.x' in one manifest and '4.2.0' in another while the lockfile says '4.2.3'. Explain how to search these files consistently and which value describes the running system.
reasoning: Different files legitimately record different things: a range, a pin, and a resolution. A search that treats them as competing claims produces false contradictions. The runtime answer is the installed artifact, which none of the three files guarantee.
answer: Search across the relevant files at once, 'git grep -n "\"acme-sdk\"" -- package.json */package.json *.lock package-lock.json pnpm-lock.yaml', and interpret each hit by its file's role rather than expecting agreement. Establish what is installed by resolving the module and reading its version, for example 'node -p "require(\"acme-sdk/package.json\").version"', and compare with the lockfile resolution. Verify by checking for multiple copies, since a nested duplicate can mean two versions load at once.

instruction: The same key must change in six '.env*' files that differ in other ways. Explain how to apply the edit so you can prove only the intended line changed in each file.
reasoning: Multi-file edits risk collateral changes, especially when files have unrelated drift. The safety property is not the command but the ability to review a bounded diff afterwards. Version control makes the review possible only if the tree was clean beforehand.
answer: Confirm 'git status --porcelain' is empty, list the files with 'git grep -l KEY -- ".env*"', apply the change with a scoped edit, then run 'git diff --stat' expecting exactly six files and 'git diff -U0' to confirm one changed line per file. Verify no other key was rewritten by diffing the sorted keys before and after, and re-run the search for the old value to confirm zero remaining matches, remembering that ignored env files may need an explicit path.

instruction: You must add a middleware line immediately after the last 'app.use' call in a file with several similar calls. Explain how to make the insertion verifiable rather than position-dependent.
reasoning: Inserting by line number breaks as soon as the file changes, and matching the first similar line can place code in the wrong order, which for middleware determines request handling semantics. Anchoring on stable syntax and then verifying placement converts a fragile edit into a checked one. Order is part of correctness here.
answer: Anchor the insertion on unique surrounding text, for example a targeted edit tool or 'awk' with a pattern, and never on a remembered line number. Then verify by reading the enclosing function, confirming the new call sits at the intended position relative to body parsers and error handlers, since Express middleware order is significant. Verify behaviourally by sending a request that should trigger the middleware and confirming its log line.

instruction: You need to change a value in a JSONC configuration file that contains comments. Explain why loading and re-writing the file with 'jq' is unsafe and what tool preserves the file.
reasoning: jq parses JSON, which discards comments and rewrites formatting, so a one-key edit becomes a whole-file change that defeats review and may break a file the consumer expects to be commented. A round trip through a lossy parser is a silent modification. Edit-in-place with a comment-aware tool preserves everything else.
answer: Use a comment-aware editor: an ast-grep or JSONC-capable tool, or a targeted text edit of just that line, keeping the surrounding bytes identical. Avoid 'jq . file > file' style round trips and never write back the parsed output. Verify with 'git diff' that exactly one line changed, and if you must reformat, do it in a separate commit so the semantic change stays reviewable.

instruction: A dependency needs a version bump. Explain why hand-editing the lockfile is the wrong modification and what sequence produces a consistent state.
reasoning: A lockfile encodes resolution, integrity hashes and transitive relationships. Changing a version string leaves hashes and dependents inconsistent, so the install either fails or silently resolves something else. Consistency must be produced by the resolver rather than asserted by an editor. The file is derived, and edits to derived files are undone by the next generation.
answer: Change the manifest, then let the package manager rewrite the lockfile: 'npm install dep@^5.2.0' or the equivalent for the manager identified from the repository's lockfile, and commit both files together. Never edit hashes or resolutions by hand. Verify with 'npm ls dep' and by confirming the lockfile entry and integrity fields changed only for the affected packages, reviewing 'git diff' on the lockfile for unrelated churn.

instruction: You must patch a library bug. Options are editing the file inside node_modules, forking the package, or using a patch file generated by the toolchain. Argue for the approach that survives a clean install.
reasoning: node_modules is derived state that any install replaces, so an edit there is invisible to teammates and CI and will be lost without warning. Forking is a durable but heavy option that changes maintenance ownership. A recorded patch keeps the change reviewable and reproducible.
answer: Use a patch workflow: make the minimal edit, generate a diff with the tooling such as 'npx patch-package <pkg>', which writes a version-specific patch into the repository, and add a postinstall hook so it reapplies after install. Record the upstream issue and remove the patch when fixed. Verify with 'rm -rf node_modules && npm ci' and confirming the patch reapplies and the bug stays fixed.

instruction: A sed command 's|.*proxy.*|proxy_pass https://new.host;|' rewrote more lines than intended in an nginx configuration. Explain the mechanism and the corrected approach.
reasoning: An unanchored greedy dot star consumes the entire line, so the pattern matches far more than the intended value, and the replacement overwrites surrounding syntax. A substitution scoped to the token, not the line, is what preserves structure. Rewriting a config line wholesale risks deleting directives sharing that line.
answer: Replace the token only and anchor the pattern, for example 'sed -n "s|proxy_pass https://old\.host|proxy_pass https://new.host|p" file.conf' to preview, then apply. For structural edits prefer a real parser or a targeted edit tool over regex over config files. Verify by diffing the file, confirming only the intended directives changed, and running 'nginx -t' to confirm the configuration still parses.

instruction: A file's watcher restarts the dev server on every save, and your multi-edit session triggered dozens of restarts and a corrupt intermediate state. Explain the safer editing strategy while a server watches the tree.
reasoning: Watchers treat every filesystem event as a signal to rebuild, so partial or incremental writes are observed as valid states, producing restart storms and confusing errors. Making edits atomic and pausing the watcher removes that interference. Understanding the observer changes how you write.
answer: Write the complete file in one atomic operation, meaning write to a temporary file then rename it into place, so the watcher sees one consistent state. Where a tool offers it, pause or scope the watcher during bulk edits, or edit on a copy and move files into place. Verify by checking the server log for a single reload and confirming the served output reflects all edits, rather than an intermediate state.

instruction: You need to create 'config/local.yaml' which might already exist and is ignored by git. Explain how to create it without clobbering anything and how to verify afterwards.
reasoning: A file that git ignores is invisible to review, so an accidental overwrite leaves no diff and no recovery path. The absence of a tracked copy means version control cannot undo the change. Creation must therefore be guarded, not merely directed.
answer: Test first: 'test -e config/local.yaml && echo exists || echo absent', and if it exists read it before writing anything. Create with a redirect only after confirming absence, or write to a temporary path and move it into place with 'mv -n' so an existing file is never replaced. Verify by re-reading the file and diffing it against the intended content, and confirm 'git status' stays clean, which shows the file remains ignored as expected.

instruction: A file must be modified inside a container running as a different user, and your editor cannot write it. Explain the sequence of checks before escalating or changing ownership.
reasoning: Permission friction is often a signal that you are editing the wrong copy or the wrong environment, not a problem to bypass. Changing ownership of mounted files can alter what the host and other processes see. The safe sequence inspects identity before escalating.
answer: Identify first: check the file's owner and mode with 'ls -l', the effective user with 'id', and whether the path is a bind mount from the host by comparing inode numbers. If it is a mount, edit on the host so ownership stays consistent. Prefer the container's own user, for example 'docker compose exec -u node', over sudo, and avoid chown on shared mounts. Verify by re-reading the file inside the container to confirm the change is visible and that the service reloads correctly.

instruction: You must append an object to a JSON array stored in a file. Explain why text append is unsafe and what modification preserves validity.
reasoning: Appending raw text ignores the closing bracket and trailing comma rules, producing a syntactically invalid file that the reader rejects later, far from the cause. Structural edits must go through a parser that maintains the format. Validity should be checked as part of the edit, not by the next consumer.
answer: Rewrite through a JSON-aware tool, for example 'jq ". + [NEW_OBJECT]" file > tmp && mv tmp file', and keep a backup or rely on a clean git state. Validate immediately with 'jq empty file' or the language's parser. Verify by re-reading the file and confirming the array length grew by exactly one, since a partial write can silently duplicate or drop entries.

instruction: A rename of 'getUserId' to 'getCurrentUserId' must not touch strings, CSS class names or documentation. Explain the editing approach and the review step that catches overreach.
reasoning: Text substitution cannot distinguish an identifier from an identically spelled string. So a rename becomes a content edit, which is how a mechanical change turns into a behaviour change. A symbol-aware rename resolves references, and diff review is what bounds the result. The verification is about the shape of the diff, not its size.
answer: Prefer a language-server rename, which edits only resolved references, and fall back to a scoped regex only if you can anchor it, for example word boundaries plus an exclusion of string literals. Then review 'git diff' hunk by hunk, checking that no changed line is inside quotes or a doc comment. Verify with a type check and the test suite, and re-run the old-name search to confirm no live references remain, accepting that dynamic references may still exist.

instruction: Autoformat on save reformatted 400 lines of a file in which you changed four. Explain how to keep the intended change reviewable and what repository-level decision resolves the conflict.
reasoning: Unformatted files combined with formatter-on-save create noise that buries the semantic change and can break bisectability. The fix is to separate formatting from behaviour so both are visible, which is a repository convention rather than a per-edit trick. A reviewer who cannot see the change cannot verify it.
answer: Stage only the intended hunk or apply formatting in a separate commit, for example reverting the file and reapplying just your edits, then running the formatter as its own commit. Establish or follow the repository convention so formatter and configuration agree, checking for a config file, an editorconfig, and a lint script that CI runs. Verify by confirming 'git diff' shows only the semantic change in the behaviour commit.

instruction: You must fix a file that still contains merge conflict markers. Explain what to establish before editing and how to verify the resolution is complete.
reasoning: A conflict is a decision record: each side encodes an intent, and choosing one side silently discards the other. Editing the text without understanding which change is authoritative risks losing a fix that only exists on one side. The markers are the symptom, not the decision.
answer: Establish the provenance with 'git status', and if the conflict is from an in-progress merge read 'git log --oneline MERGE_HEAD' and both sides' commits before choosing. Resolve by keeping both intents where compatible, and verify no markers remain with 'rg -n "^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)" .'. Confirm the file parses with the appropriate check, then run the tests for that module, since a syntactically valid resolution can still be semantically wrong.

instruction: You need to change a SQL migration that was already applied in production. Explain why editing it is unsafe and what the correct modification is.
reasoning: Applied migrations are identified by checksum or revision state, so editing history breaks verification for every environment that already ran it and can make later deployments refuse to apply. The schema's current state, not the file's text, determines what the fix must do. New intent requires a new migration.
answer: Do not edit the applied file. Read the live schema state, for example psql's '\d table' and the migrations ledger, then author a new migration that transforms the current state to the intended state. Verify locally by resetting a scratch database and running the full chain, confirming the new migration applies cleanly and the resulting schema matches the model. If the migration was never applied anywhere, coordinate with the team before touching history.

instruction: A script must write a configuration file that other processes read continuously. Explain the write strategy that avoids exposing a partial file and why the naive redirect is unsafe.
reasoning: Truncating and then writing makes the file briefly empty or partial, so a concurrent reader can see incomplete content that parses as a different configuration. Atomic replacement via rename is the standard mechanism because renames are atomic on the same filesystem. The choice of write strategy is a correctness decision.
answer: Write to a temporary file in the same directory, flush and close it, then rename it over the target with 'mv tmp target', so readers observe either the old or new content. Set permissions before the rename, and re-read the target to confirm content. Verify by running the consumer during a write and confirming no parse error, and use 'lsof' to see who holds the file if the update is not observed.

instruction: You must delete a directory named 'uploads' from the container image, but the same name is a mounted volume in development. Explain the inspection that prevents destructive overreach.
reasoning: Recursive deletion through a mount point can remove host data that the image does not own, and the path is indistinguishable from a plain directory by name alone. Mounts and links change what a deletion means. Confirming the filesystem topology is a precondition, not an optional extra.
answer: Inspect before deleting: 'findmnt' or 'mount | grep uploads', and compare device and inode with 'stat -c "%d %i %n"' against the parent, which distinguishes a mount from a directory. Check whether it is a symlink to elsewhere with 'readlink -f', since deleting through a link follows it. Verify by deleting the contents rather than the directory, or by unmounting first, and confirm the host path is untouched afterwards.

instruction: An untracked file 'notes.md' is shadowed by a .gitignore pattern and you want it versioned. Explain how to determine the cause and the two different fixes with different consequences.
reasoning: Ignore patterns are often broad, so a file is excluded by accident and the author believes it was committed. Forcing a specific file in contradicts the pattern's intent, while narrowing the pattern changes what else becomes tracked. Both are legitimate but have different blast radii, so the pattern must be understood first.
answer: Find the offending rule with 'git check-ignore -v notes.md', which reports the file and line of the matching pattern, and review the surrounding patterns to see the rule's purpose. Then either narrow the pattern and add a negation for this path, or accept the file being ignored and place it in a versioned directory. Verify with 'git status' and 'git ls-files --error-unmatch notes.md' after staging, and check what else the narrowed pattern starts tracking.

instruction: You need to fix indentation of a nested list in a YAML manifest. Explain how to verify the edit semantically rather than by looking at the file.
reasoning: YAML assigns meaning through indentation, so a visual diff and a parse check are different evidence, and a change can look right while reparenting a key. Validating the parsed structure confirms intent. Textual correctness is not semantic correctness for indentation-sensitive formats.
answer: After editing, compare parsed output before and after, for example 'yq eval . manifest.yaml' or 'python3 -c "import yaml,sys;print(yaml.safe_load(open(sys.argv[1])))" manifest.yaml', and diff the two structures rather than the files. Confirm the key landed under the intended parent and that list items remained a sequence. Verify with the consumer's validation, for example 'kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f' or the compose equivalent.

instruction: Another process may still be writing to a file you are about to edit. Explain how to determine whether concurrent writes are happening and what to do if they are.
reasoning: Concurrent writers produce interleaved content and lost updates, and an editor's save can overwrite bytes appended after it was opened. Detecting another writer is therefore part of a safe edit, not paranoia. The right action changes from editing to coordination once a writer exists.
answer: Check open handles with 'lsof <file>' or 'fuser <file>' and inspect the modification time over a few seconds to see whether it grows. Compare your copy with the current content before saving, since an editor that opened the file earlier may hold a stale buffer. If a writer exists, stop it, lock the file, or edit through the owning process rather than saving over it, and verify by checksumming after the edit.

instruction: You want to remove unused imports flagged by a linter's autofix from a file that also has real logic changes. Explain the sequencing that keeps both reviewable and safe.
reasoning: Mixing an automatic cleanup with hand-written logic in one change makes the diff hard to verify. An autofix can alter evaluation order or remove imports that carry side effects. Separating the steps lets each be checked independently. Sequencing is a safety measure when a tool edits code for you.
answer: Commit or stash the logic change first, then run the autofix alone and inspect its diff, checking especially for side-effectful imports such as polyfills or CSS imports whose removal changes behaviour. Re-run the build and tests after each step rather than once at the end. Verify by confirming the two commits individually pass CI, which localises any regression to one kind of change.

instruction: Your editor shows you opened 'config/app.json' but after saving, the shared template used by four services changed. Explain the file property responsible and how to make an isolated change.
reasoning: Editing a symlink writes through to the target, so a change intended for one consumer alters every service that resolves to the same file. The path you opened is not necessarily the object you modified. Checking link status before saving is what prevents an unintended shared change.
answer: Inspect with 'ls -l config/app.json' and 'readlink -f config/app.json' to see the real target and how many names reach it. To change one service only, replace the link with an independent copy, for example 'cp --remove-destination target config/app.json' after confirming that is the intended design, or introduce an override file if the configuration system supports layering. Verify by diffing the shared template against its original to confirm it is untouched, and by reloading one service to confirm it sees your change.

instruction: You renamed 'components/UserCard.tsx' to 'components/userCard.tsx' locally with no visible change, and the build now fails only on Linux CI. Explain the filesystem mechanism and the safe rename procedure.
reasoning: A case-insensitive filesystem treats the two names as the same file, so the working tree looks correct while the index records nothing, and the case-sensitive CI checkout produces a different result. Renaming through git's index makes the change explicit and platform independent. Local success is not evidence that the repository recorded the rename.
answer: Rename through git so the index records it: 'git mv components/UserCard.tsx components/userCard.tsx', or if the working tree is confused, 'git mv -f' or a two-step rename through a temporary name. Then update import specifiers, since case-sensitive resolution also affects imports. Verify by checking 'git status' shows a rename, and by cloning the branch into a case-sensitive location or relying on CI to confirm resolution, plus running the build.

instruction: You have a patch from a colleague for a working tree with your own uncommitted edits. Explain the checks before applying and how to apply it so that reverting is easy.
reasoning: Applying a patch to a modified tree can fail partially or land on the wrong context, and a plain apply with force options can corrupt your work. Verifying applicability first, and applying in a way that keeps a clean undo path, turns a risky operation into a controlled one. The safety comes from the sequence, not from a flag.
answer: Verify the tree with 'git status', then test with 'git apply --check patch.diff' and, if it fails, retry with 'git apply --3way' so conflicts are recorded as conflicts rather than skipped. Prefer a scratch worktree or 'git stash' plus a clean apply so your edits stay recoverable. Inspect 'git diff' after applying, and revert with 'git apply -R patch.diff' if needed. Verify by confirming no rejected hunks remain and by running the tests the patch was meant to satisfy.

instruction: 'sed -i s/a/b/ config.json' left the file zero bytes after the disk filled mid-write. Explain the mechanism and the safer editing pattern.
reasoning: In-place editing typically truncates the original and writes a replacement, so an interrupted write leaves an empty or partial file with no backup, and the previous content is unrecoverable if it was untracked. Editing to a temporary file and renaming makes failure non-destructive. Atomicity is a property of the write strategy.
answer: Prefer temp-then-move, which is what version-controlled editors effectively give you: 'sed "s/a/b/" config.json > config.json.tmp && mv config.json.tmp config.json', and check 'df -h' before large rewrites. Keep a backup, 'sed -i.bak', when no VCS state exists. Verify by validating the file parses after the edit, and recover this incident from a backup, an editor buffer or a rebuild rather than retrying the same in-place command.

instruction: A key must be added to a .env file without exposing the value in shell history, terminal output or logs. Explain the command construction that satisfies this and what to verify afterwards.
reasoning: Redirecting an echoed secret writes it into history and often into captured logs, and arguments passed on a command line are visible to other processes. The value should reach the file through a channel that does not print or list it. Handling secrets is part of the edit, not an afterthought.
answer: Write without echoing, for example using a here-document with restrictive umask, 'umask 077 && cat >> .env' so you type the line without it appearing in history, or generate the value directly into the file. Never pass the secret as a command argument. Verify by checking 'ls -l .env' permissions, confirming the key parses, and grepping history and logs for the value; if it leaked, rotate it rather than deleting the line.

instruction: The vendored vendor.css contains a rule you need to override. Explain why editing the vendored file is the wrong modification and what change achieves the goal durably.
reasoning: Vendored assets are replaced by updates or by a package install, so a hand edit there is lost and creates a difference nobody can explain later. Overrides exist precisely to avoid mutating third-party files. The right target is your own layer, with specificity or source order as the mechanism.
answer: Do not edit vendor.css. Add an override in your own stylesheet with a selector that wins by source order or specificity, or configure the build to post-process the dependency through a documented step. Confirm which stylesheet loads last by inspecting the built HTML or CSS bundle order, since order determines the outcome. Verify by inspecting the computed styles in the browser to confirm the override applied, and by re-running the install to show your change survives.

instruction: You want to run the formatter across the whole repository so future diffs are clean. Explain the sequencing and commit boundaries that make the change safe.
reasoning: A repository-wide format commit touches every file, which destroys blame granularity and can collide with in-flight branches, so it must be isolated from behaviour changes and coordinated. Mixing it with a functional change makes review impossible. The plan is a workflow decision, not a formatting decision.
answer: Ensure no concurrent work, commit the formatting alone with a message that names it, and mark it in the repository's ignore-revs file so blame can skip it. Split by directory if the project is large so review is feasible. Verify by confirming 'git diff --stat' shows only whitespace or formatting and that a type check and the test suite pass, then rebase open branches promptly.

instruction: You plan to delete 'tests/fixtures/sample-data/' because the tests appear to ignore it. Explain the evidence you need before deleting a fixture directory.
reasoning: Fixtures are frequently loaded by path strings, by directory globbing, or by snapshot comparisons. So a name-based reference search finds nothing and the deletion still breaks tests. Absence of an import is not absence of a dependency. The cheap verification is running the suite after deletion on a branch.
answer: Search for path fragments rather than the directory name alone, for example 'rg -n "sample-data|fixtures/" tests', and check configuration that sets a fixture root or a glob. Then delete on a branch, run the full suite including snapshot and integration tests, and confirm nothing regressed. Verify with 'git status' before committing so you can restore immediately, and record any file the suite still needs even though it appears unused.

instruction: You need to add an npm script. Explain how to modify package.json safely and why a text edit of that file invites a specific class of error.
reasoning: A manifest is strict JSON used by the toolchain, so a stray comma or quote breaks every command afterwards, and the failure appears as a parse error unrelated to your intent. Command-based mutation avoids hand-managing syntax. Validation closes the loop.
answer: Use 'npm pkg set scripts.test="vitest run"', which rewrites the JSON correctly, or edit carefully and validate immediately with 'node -e "require(\"./package.json\")"' or 'jq . package.json'. Check whether the key belongs in scripts, devDependencies or a tool-specific section by reading the tool's documentation. Verify by running the script exactly as CI will, and review 'git diff' to confirm only the intended key changed.

instruction: A shared CI workflow file is used by twelve repositories and you need to change a step for one project. Explain the modification strategy and the safety reasoning.
reasoning: Editing a template consumed by many repositories converts a local need into a global change. So the blast radius must be reduced by parameterising rather than special-casing, and by verifying with a single consumer first. The safe direction is to widen capability without changing defaults. Recognising shared state is the key inference.
answer: Prefer adding an opt-in input with a default that preserves current behaviour, then set it only in the repository that needs it, rather than altering the default for everyone. Test by bumping a reference in one consuming repository and watching that run, not the other eleven. Verify by diffing behaviour on a second consumer after wider adoption, and keep the change reversible by recording the previous version reference.

instruction: A teammate asks you to hand-edit the built JavaScript in 'dist/' to test a fix quickly. Explain why that verification is unreliable and what the alternative is.
reasoning: Editing derived output can confirm a hypothesis about the runtime, but any rebuild, watcher or deployment replaces it, so a passing result proves the theory rather than the fix. It also risks committing an artifact. The correct framing separates throwaway diagnosis from durable change.
answer: Treat a dist edit only as a time-boxed experiment, clearly labelled and never committed, and reproduce the same change in source with a rebuild so the observation is verified through the real pipeline. Confirm the artifact is regenerated by checking 'git check-ignore dist' and the build script, and by watching the file change when you rebuild. Verify the actual fix in source with the tests that cover the behaviour.

instruction: Two git worktrees share the same repository and you change a setting in the common git directory to fix one of them. Explain the file-level consequence.
reasoning: Worktrees split the working tree but share configuration, hooks and refs under the common directory, so an edit there silently alters every linked checkout. Knowing which files are shared determines whether a fix belongs in the common or per-worktree scope. The failure mode is fixing one checkout while breaking another.
answer: Check 'git rev-parse --git-common-dir' and '--absolute-git-dir' to see which directory you are editing, and make per-worktree settings in the worktree-specific config with 'git config --worktree key value'. Use 'git config --list --show-origin' to see which file each value came from before writing. Verify by re-running the command in the other worktree and confirming it is unaffected.

instruction: You are about to delete files listed by 'git clean -fdx' to get a pristine tree while a build is half-finished. Explain the safer sequence.
reasoning: The 'x' flag removes ignored files, which include local configuration, secrets and caches that no version control can restore. A clean tree is a means, not a goal, and here a rebuild may be all that is needed. Destructive convenience commands deserve an explicit preview step.
answer: Preview first with 'git clean -nd' and then '-ndx' to see exactly what would be removed, and exclude paths you need, for example 'git clean -fdx -e .env -e node_modules'. Prefer targeted deletion of the offending artifact over a global clean. Verify the intended outcome, a correct build, by rebuilding after the narrower deletion. Never run the destructive form to make a symptom disappear without understanding it.

instruction: You edited a file, tests now fail, and the file is untracked so git cannot restore it. Explain the recovery options and what to do before trying another edit.
reasoning: Recovery of untracked content is limited to copies that actually exist, so the first step is enumerating them rather than continuing to edit, which destroys the only remaining version. Editor backups, build outputs and caches may hold the previous content. Pausing preserves options.
answer: Stop editing and look for a copy: an editor local history or backup file, the same file inside a build cache or container layer, a previous build output, or a branch or stash entry. Compare candidates before overwriting. Verify the recovered version by re-running the tests, then immediately add the file to version control or create a backup, and treat the gap as a process lesson about working with untracked files.

instruction: A configuration file is a hard link to a shared defaults file rather than a symlink, so your editor changed the defaults for everyone. Explain why hard links are harder to detect than symlinks and how to check.
reasoning: Hard-linked files look like ordinary files at the path, so nothing in a directory listing shows the aliasing; only link count and inode identity reveal it. An editor that writes in place mutates the shared inode, whereas one that replaces the file breaks the link and changes only your path. The write strategy determines the blast radius.
answer: Check with 'stat -c "%i %h %n"' on both paths and compare inodes, and look for a link count above one. Edit by writing a new file and renaming it over the path, which detaches your copy while leaving the shared file intact, or copy the file to make it independent first. Verify by confirming the shared defaults' inode and checksum are unchanged after your edit.

instruction: You must remove a file from version control while keeping it on disk, because it was committed accidentally but is needed locally. Explain the correct command and the follow-up that prevents recurrence.
reasoning: Deleting the file accomplishes the wrong goal, since local content is needed, while ignoring it alone changes nothing because tracked files are unaffected by ignore rules. Untracking is a distinct operation from deleting and from ignoring. Understanding these three states separately is what makes the fix correct.
answer: Use 'git rm --cached path' to remove it from the index only, then add the path to .gitignore, remembering that ignore rules do not apply to already-tracked files. If the file ever contained secrets, treat it as disclosed: rotation is the response, since history still holds it. Verify with 'git ls-files path' returning nothing, 'git status' showing the file as ignored, and the file still present on disk.

instruction: A one-line change is needed in a file that is also modified by a background formatter. Explain how to detect interference and make your change stick.
reasoning: Concurrent automated editors produce a write race where the later save wins, which looks like your change vanishing at random. Detecting the other writer is the diagnosis; racing it again is not a fix. Stability of the file's modification time is the observable.
answer: Watch for concurrent writes by sampling the file's modification time or checksum over a few seconds, and check running processes for a formatting watcher with 'ps aux' filtered by name. Pause the watcher, apply your edit, re-run the formatter once, and confirm both changes coexist, which means the configuration is compatible. Verify by checksumming the file after the formatter runs and by reading the diff to confirm your line survived.

instruction: A codemod you generated edits 1,800 files. Explain how to review the result before committing and what makes a mechanical change trustworthy.
reasoning: Large automated edits are trusted by default, which is exactly when a systematic error propagates everywhere. Review must be structured by sampling and by grouping changes, and trust comes from independent verification such as a build, not from the size of the diff. Mechanical does not mean correct.
answer: Run the codemod on a branch with a clean tree, then review by category: 'git diff --stat' to see which kinds of files changed, inspect a stratified sample of five to ten files including edge cases such as strings and comments, and re-run the search for the old pattern to confirm completeness. Follow with a type check, build and full test run. Verify by checking that no changes landed in generated or vendored paths, and split unrelated formatting into its own commit.

instruction: You are on 'feature/cart' with uncommitted edits and must urgently fix a bug on 'main'. Explain the decision process for moving work without losing anything, comparing branch switching, stashing and a worktree.
reasoning: Each option moves state differently: a branch switch carries modifications and can fail, stashing removes them from the tree where they can be forgotten or lost on a conflict, and a worktree leaves the current tree untouched. The right choice depends on how long the fix takes and whether the current work must keep running. Safety here is about recoverability, not convenience.
answer: Prefer 'git worktree add ../hotfix main' so the cart edits and any running dev server stay intact, then fix and commit in the new directory. If you must switch branches, first check 'git status', and either commit a work-in-progress commit or stash with 'git stash push -u -m "cart wip"' so untracked files are included and the entry is identifiable. Verify afterwards with 'git stash list' and by returning to 'feature/cart' and confirming 'git status' shows your edits restored.

instruction: After resolving conflicts you ran 'git stash pop', and git reported a conflict while keeping the stash entry. A teammate says the pop failed so the work is lost. Correct them and explain how to verify the actual state.
reasoning: A pop that conflicts deliberately retains the stash entry, so the work exists in two places rather than none, and the failure is about the index state, not about data loss. Reading git's message carefully is what distinguishes a recovery task from a panic. Verification comes from inspecting both the tree and the stash list.
answer: Explain that 'git stash pop' only drops the entry when it applies cleanly, so a conflicted pop leaves 'stash@{0}' intact. Resolve the conflicts, check 'git status' for unmerged paths, and drop the entry yourself with 'git stash drop' once satisfied. If you want to inspect without applying, use 'git stash show -p'. Verify by diffing the working tree against the stash entry to confirm nothing is missing before dropping.

instruction: A deploy script takes a commit hash from the ticket, but 'git tag --points-at <hash>' returns nothing and the release tag points at a different hash. Explain what you must establish before deploying anything.
reasoning: A tag names a commit, and two different commits can contain similar work without being identical. The question is not which label is prettier but whether the tested change is an ancestor of the thing being deployed. Ancestry is verifiable; assumption is not.
answer: Compare the two commits with 'git merge-base --is-ancestor <hash> <tag-commit>' and read the difference with 'git log --oneline <hash>..<tag-commit>'. If the ticket's commit is not contained in the tag, either the tag is newer, in which case verify the change is still present with 'git show <tag>:path/to/file', or the change is missing and deploying the tag would ship a regression. Verify by diffing the deployed artifact's version metadata against the commit you intended before promoting.

instruction: You ran 'git checkout -- src/price.ts' to discard a hunk and now need the discarded edits. Explain what git can and cannot recover here, and the realistic avenues.
reasoning: Discarding a tracked file restores the index or committed content, and unstaged work that was never added is not in the object database, so git has nothing to recover. Dangling blobs exist only for content that was staged at least once. Knowing which of those states applied determines whether recovery is possible at all.
answer: Check whether the file was ever staged, because staged content leaves a blob reachable via 'git fsck --lost-found' or 'git cat-file' on dangling objects, and search those blobs for your text. Otherwise look in editor local history, build caches, a container layer, or a CI artifact from a run that included the file. Verify any recovered version by diffing it against the current file before accepting it. As prevention, use 'git add -p' for partial work or commit early, since discard operations have no undo.

instruction: A rebase onto main produced conflicts in six files and you suspect the rebase plan itself is wrong. Explain the decision between continuing, aborting and restarting differently, and why 'skip' is dangerous here.
reasoning: Conflicts during a rebase can indicate either ordinary divergence or a misunderstanding of which commits should be replayed. Skipping drops a commit silently, which converts a merge problem into lost work. Aborting is cheap and reversible, so it dominates guessing when the plan is doubtful.
answer: Inspect the plan first: 'git rebase --onto' arguments and 'git log --oneline main..HEAD' show which commits are being replayed, and 'git status' lists conflicted paths. If the intended base was wrong, run 'git rebase --abort', which returns you to the pre-rebase state verifiable with 'git reflog', and restart with the correct base. Resolve conflicts file by file and stage them, continuing with 'git rebase --continue'. Verify at the end by comparing the tree with the pre-rebase commit using 'git diff ORIG_HEAD HEAD', expecting only intended differences.

instruction: You need to update a shared branch after rebasing locally. A teammate suggests 'git push --force'. Explain the specific risk and the safer formulation plus the check that must precede it.
reasoning: A blind force push overwrites commits other people have pushed since your last fetch, deleting their work from the branch with no conflict warning. The safer form checks whether the remote moved as you expected, converting an unconditional overwrite into a conditional one. Even then, coordination matters because history rewriting affects everyone.
answer: Fetch first and inspect what would be lost with 'git log --oneline HEAD..origin/branch'; if it is non-empty, integrate those commits rather than overwrite. Then push with 'git push --force-with-lease', which fails if the remote does not match your expected state, and announce the rewrite so others can rebase onto the new tip. Verify by confirming no remote commits were discarded and by checking that teammates' branches are rebased rather than reset.

instruction: You committed a fix to 'main' locally when it belonged on 'fix/typo'. Nothing is pushed. Explain the command sequence that moves the commit and leaves main pristine, and how you verify both outcomes.
reasoning: The goal has two parts: the commit must exist on the correct branch and must no longer exist on the wrong one. Cherry-picking satisfies the first, and a reset satisfies the second, but the reset is destructive if the hash is wrong, so the state must be recorded first. Verification is per branch, not global.
answer: Note the hash with 'git log -1 --format=%H', create or switch to the target branch and 'git cherry-pick <hash>', then return to main and 'git reset --hard HEAD~1', which is safe here only because nothing was pushed and the commit is preserved by the cherry-pick. Verify with 'git log --oneline -3' on both branches, confirming the fix appears on 'fix/typo' and that main's tip matches origin/main, and re-run 'git status' to confirm no other changes were reset.

instruction: A file that existed three releases ago was deleted and you must restore its content into the current tree. Explain how to retrieve it without disturbing your work and what to check before re-adding it.
reasoning: Old content is reachable by revision, so recovery does not require a checkout that would disturb the working tree. Re-adding a deleted file blindly can reintroduce a component nothing imports or that was removed for a reason. Retrieval and reintegration are separate decisions.
answer: Find the last revision containing it with 'git log --diff-filter=D --oneline -- path/to/file', then read the previous version with 'git show <sha>^:path/to/file'. Write it out to the path without switching branches. Before committing, check whether anything references it and whether its dependencies still exist, since a restored file may import deleted modules. Verify by building and by grepping for references, and confirm 'git status' shows the file as added rather than as an unrelated modification.

instruction: Your tests are failing and you believe a recent change caused it. Explain how to set up 'git bisect' correctly, including the two preconditions that are commonly skipped.
reasoning: Bisect moves HEAD repeatedly, so uncommitted work would be carried across revisions or block the operation entirely, and an unreliable test script produces a confidently wrong commit. Preparing a clean tree and a deterministic, exit-code-based script is what makes the search valid. The tool is only as good as its harness.
answer: Stash or commit local work, verify 'git status' is clean, and write a script that exits 0 for good and non-zero for bad, covering the exact failure, then sanity-check it on known-good and known-bad revisions. Start with 'git bisect start HEAD <known-good>' and 'git bisect run ./check.sh'. Also test the behaviour once per revision to catch flakiness, since a nondeterministic result misleads the search. Verify the identified commit by checking out its parent and confirming the failure disappears.

instruction: 'git blame' on a file in a CI-cloned repository shows a single commit for every line. Explain the clone configuration likely responsible and how to confirm it.
reasoning: Shallow and filtered clones retain only part of history, so blame, log and bisect silently operate on incomplete data. The output looks authoritative rather than truncated, which is what makes it dangerous. Clone depth is an environment property that changes the meaning of any history query.
answer: Check whether the repository is shallow with 'git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository', and inspect 'git log --oneline | tail -3' to see whether history stops abruptly at a clone boundary. Confirm CI's fetch depth in the workflow file. Fix by fetching more history, for example 'git fetch --unshallow' or a larger fetch-depth, and verify by re-running blame and confirming older commits appear. Record that any earlier bisect or blame result was inconclusive rather than evidence.

instruction: A pull created a merge commit you did not want and your branch now has tangled history. Explain how to assess the damage before rewriting anything, and the options depending on whether the branch was pushed.
reasoning: Rewriting pushed history affects everyone who based work on it, so the decision to clean up depends on publication state, not on aesthetics. Inspecting ancestry and remote tracking tells you which options are safe. Undo operations are cheap locally and expensive publicly.
answer: Look at 'git log --graph --oneline -10' and compare with 'git rev-parse origin/<branch>' to see whether the merge commit is public. If local only, undo with 'git reset --hard <pre-merge-commit>' found in 'git reflog', then integrate with 'git rebase origin/main'. If pushed, do not rewrite; continue normally, or coordinate the rewrite and force-push with lease. Verify by confirming the intended commits are all present with 'git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD' and that no work was dropped.
