instruction: You want to see whether a change exists on the release branch without checking it out. Explain which command answers it and why 'git diff' against the branch can mislead.
reasoning: A plain diff compares endpoints, so a change can be absent from the diff because later edits reversed or moved it, while the commit itself was never merged. Distinguishing 'the commit is present' from 'the content matches' requires a different query. Both questions are legitimate and need different tools.
answer: Test commit membership with 'git branch --contains <sha>' or 'git tag --contains <sha>', and search history with 'git log --oneline release/2026-09..HEAD' versus the reverse range. Use 'git cherry -v origin/release <sha>' to see whether the change was applied, including as a rebased variant with a different hash. Verify by reading the target file at that revision with 'git show release/2026-09:path/to/file'.

instruction: Before pushing you want to review every change the push will deliver, not just the last commit. Explain the commands and why reviewing 'git diff HEAD~1' is inadequate.
reasoning: A branch may carry several commits plus earlier ones the reviewer never saw, and a single-commit diff omits them entirely. The push delivers a range, so review must be scoped to that range. Wrong scope is how unintended commits reach a shared branch.
answer: Review the outgoing range: 'git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD' to list commits, 'git diff origin/main...HEAD --stat' for the file summary, and 'git diff origin/main...HEAD' for content, using the three-dot form so you compare against the merge base rather than a moving tip. Verify that no unrelated commits are included, and confirm the remote has not advanced with 'git fetch --dry-run' or a status check before pushing.

instruction: You want to prepare a release and are offered a lightweight tag or an annotated tag. Explain the difference in the information recorded and which supports auditing a deployment.
reasoning: A lightweight tag is a ref pointing at a commit, while an annotated object records a tagger, date, message and optional signature. Auditing who released what and when depends on that extra metadata, which cannot be added later without retagging. The choice determines whether the release is explainable after the fact.
answer: Use 'git tag -a v1.8.0 -m "release notes summary"' and push it explicitly, since tags are not included in a normal push, and sign it if the project's policy expects verification. Then confirm the tag object's contents with 'git cat-file -p v1.8.0' and check it points at the tested commit. Verify the deployment by reading the released version from a build metadata endpoint rather than assuming the tag was what got deployed.

instruction: A teammate says 'git status' shows nothing even though they edited a file, and the file is not in 'git ls-files'. Explain the two candidate causes and how to distinguish them.
reasoning: An edited file can be invisible because it is ignored, or because the edit landed on a different path or in a different checkout than the one being inspected. Both produce the same empty status, and the remedies differ. Cheap checks separate them without guesswork.
answer: Test ignore status with 'git check-ignore -v <path>', which names the matching rule if that is the cause, and confirm tracking with 'git ls-files --error-unmatch <path>'. Then verify the file actually changed by checking its modification time and by 'pwd' plus 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel', which catches edits made in a different worktree or directory. Verify by making a trivial edit and re-running status after the identified cause is resolved.

instruction: You need to stage only part of a file's changes for a commit that must be revertable alone. Explain the staging workflow and how you confirm the commit contains exactly what you intend.
reasoning: Committing whole files bundles unrelated edits and destroys the ability to revert one concern. Selective staging is the mechanism, and the index is what the commit actually records. So verification must inspect the staged snapshot rather than the working tree. Reviewing the wrong diff is how unwanted changes get published.
answer: Use 'git add -p' or an editor's staging view to select hunks, and note that untracked files need 'git add -N' before they can be split. Confirm with 'git diff --cached', which shows the staged content, and compare with 'git diff' for what remains unstaged. After committing, verify with 'git show --stat HEAD' and 'git show HEAD' so the commit is reviewable as a standalone revert. Keep the working tree changes for a separate commit.

instruction: Every file in the tree appears modified in 'git status' although you changed none, immediately after changing machines. Explain the two common causes and the evidence that separates them.
reasoning: Mass modification without content change usually comes from line-ending normalisation or the executable bit being recorded differently, both of which alter git's comparison without altering visible text. The diff itself distinguishes them. Reacting by committing everything would bake an environment artifact into the repository.
answer: Inspect 'git diff --stat' and one file's diff: line-ending churn appears as every line changed, while a mode change appears as 'old mode 100644 / new mode 100755'. Confirm with 'git config core.filemode' and 'core.autocrlf', and check 'git ls-files --eol' for index and worktree line endings. Fix by setting the appropriate config or adding a .gitattributes policy, and avoid committing the noise. Verify by restoring the config and confirming status becomes clean.

instruction: You need main's latest state to start a hotfix, but your local main has not been updated and you are unsure whether it is behind. Explain how to establish the truth before branching.
reasoning: A local ref records the last state you fetched, not the remote's current tip, so branching from it can silently omit merged work. The question is answered by comparing refs after a fetch, not by trusting the name 'main'. Naming a branch does not make it current.
answer: Fetch first with 'git fetch origin', then compare with 'git rev-list --count main..origin/main' and 'main..origin/main' in both directions to see whether local is behind, ahead or diverged. Branch from the fetched ref, 'git switch -c hotfix origin/main', and confirm the base with 'git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main HEAD'. Verify by checking that the merged feature commit you expect is reachable with 'git branch --contains <sha>'.

instruction: You committed to a detached HEAD after checking out a tag for testing. Explain the risk of continuing there and the command that preserves the work.
reasoning: Detached HEAD is not referenced by a branch, so commits made there are reachable only through the reflog and become unreachable after other checkouts. Creating a branch is a trivial, non-destructive step that makes the work durable. Recognising the reference state is what prevents silent loss.
answer: Create a branch immediately at the current commit, 'git switch -c experiment-from-v1.7', which keeps the commit reachable, or 'git branch name' without moving. If you already switched away, recover with 'git reflog' and 'git branch rescue <sha>'. Verify by confirming 'git log --oneline -3' shows your commit and that it is no longer detached, checking 'git status' for the branch name.

instruction: You want to squash six commits into one before a merge, but three colleagues have based branches on this branch. Explain the decision and the alternatives.
reasoning: History cleanup improves review but rewrites commits that others reference, which forces everyone to rebase and risks lost work if they do it wrong. The cost is borne by other people, not by the person running the command. Coordination is part of the technical decision.
answer: Prefer a merge strategy that preserves history, such as a squash merge on the platform, which produces one commit on the target branch without rewriting your branch, so colleagues' bases remain valid. If you must rebase locally, announce it, ensure their work is pushed, and force-push with lease afterwards. Verify by confirming the colleagues' branches still build and that 'git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD' shows the intended single commit on the target.

instruction: A commit that is already on the shared release branch caused a regression. Compare 'git revert' and 'git reset' here and state which is acceptable and why.
reasoning: Reset removes commits from a branch's history, which rewrites shared state and breaks everyone who has the old commits, while revert adds a new commit that undoes the change and remains consistent for all clones. On published history, the additive option is the safe one. The choice depends on publication state, not on preference.
answer: Use 'git revert <sha>' on the release branch so history only grows, and verify with 'git log --oneline -3' plus a test run confirming the regression is gone. Avoid reset and force-push on a shared branch; if the branch were local-only, reset would be acceptable. Consider whether the original change should be fixed forward instead, which depends on whether the reverted commit also carried unrelated work, so read 'git show <sha>' before deciding.

instruction: You ran 'git stash drop' on the wrong entry. Explain what makes recovery possible, the commands to try, and the time pressure involved.
reasoning: Git deletes references rather than objects, so the dropped stash remains a dangling commit until garbage collection prunes it, which makes recovery a race. Knowing the window exists prevents premature resignation and also prevents careless further operations that could accelerate collection. The reflog and object database are the recovery paths.
answer: Search for the object with 'git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs | grep commit' or 'git reflog show stash', and inspect candidates with 'git show <sha>' and 'git stash show -p <sha>'. Recreate the entry with 'git stash apply <sha>' or create a branch at that commit, 'git branch rescued <sha>', to make it reachable. Verify the content matches what you lost before deleting anything else, and avoid running maintenance commands that would prune it.

instruction: A merge produced a conflict only in a submodule entry, showing two different commit hashes for 'services/payments'. Explain what the conflict actually means and how to resolve it correctly.
reasoning: A submodule conflict is not a text conflict but a disagreement about which commit of another repository the superproject should reference, so picking a side by eye can silently discard one branch's work. The correct resolution requires finding a commit in the submodule that contains both. This is a cross-repository ancestry question.
answer: Inspect both sides with 'git diff --submodule=log' to see the commit ranges each branch brought, then enter the submodule and determine whether a commit exists containing both, for example by merging or rebasing inside the submodule, and check with 'git merge-base --is-ancestor'. Update the recorded pointer with 'git add services/payments' after checking out the combined commit. Verify by running the submodule's tests and confirming 'git ls-tree HEAD services/payments' records the intended hash.

instruction: You must investigate a production bug while keeping an in-progress refactor untouched, without stashing. Explain how a second working directory helps and what it shares.
reasoning: A worktree gives an independent checkout and index while sharing the object database. So investigation can happen at another revision without touching the current tree or its running processes. Understanding that refs and objects are shared prevents surprising side effects from commits made in one tree. The tool isolates state, not history.
answer: Create it with 'git worktree add ../investigate origin/main' and read or bisect there, leaving the refactor and its dev server untouched. Remember that a branch checked out in one worktree cannot be checked out in another, and that commits made in either are immediately visible to the other through shared refs. Verify with 'git worktree list' and by confirming the original tree still shows your uncommitted refactor, then remove it with 'git worktree remove'.

instruction: You are asked to delete several local branches that look finished. Explain the check that prevents deleting real work and how to interpret its output.
reasoning: A branch is finished only relative to some integration point, so a branch that is unmerged into main may still be merged into a release branch or contain work a colleague built on. The check must ask the right target and be repeated per branch. Deleting by intuition discards the only reference to commits.
answer: List candidates with 'git branch --no-merged origin/main' and inspect each with 'git log --oneline origin/main..<branch>' to see what would be lost, and check 'git branch -r --contains <tip>' to see whether the tip is already published elsewhere. Prefer 'git branch -d', which refuses unmerged branches, over '-D', and if you must force, note the tip hash or create a backup branch first. Verify afterwards by confirming the intended work is still reachable from a remote or tag.

instruction: A cherry-picked fix must be verified as identical to the original, since the rebase applied with edits. Explain how to compare two commits and what a difference in hash means here.
reasoning: Cherry-picking creates a new commit, so differing hashes are expected and prove nothing either way. Content equivalence is what matters, and patch comparison or patch-id detects it, while metadata differences explain hash divergence. Conflating identity with equality is the reasoning error.
answer: Compare the changes with 'git show <orig>' and 'git show <pick>', or compute normalised identities with 'git patch-id' on both patches, which ignores commit metadata and context differences. A mismatch here means the resolution altered behaviour, which is worth reviewing deliberately. Verify additionally by diffing the resulting files, 'git diff <orig> <pick> -- path/to/file', and by running the test that the fix addresses.

instruction: You amended a commit that you had already pushed to a shared branch, and a colleague now reports duplicated changes. Explain what happened mechanically and how the team recovers.
reasoning: Amending rewrites the commit, so the remote's old version and your new one diverge. A subsequent merge or rebase can reapply the original changes alongside the amended ones, producing apparent duplication. The root cause is rewriting published history, not the amend command itself. Recovery is reconciliation, not another rewrite.
answer: Explain that the pre-amend commit still exists in the colleague's branch, so history contains both variants. Decide one canonical version, fix forward with a commit that removes the duplicate, or have the colleague reset their branch to the amended commit if nobody else built on it. Use 'git log --oneline --left-right origin/branch...branch' to see the divergence. Verify by confirming the final tree matches intent with a diff against the target branch and by running the affected tests.

instruction: 'git status' reports clean, yet 'git diff origin/main -- src/app.ts' shows your changes are missing and the file on disk differs from origin. Explain a git feature that produces exactly this and how to detect it.
reasoning: Git can be told to ignore changes to a tracked path locally, which makes status truthful from git's perspective while the file genuinely differs. This is common for configuration files edited for local testing. Without checking the flag, an agent concludes the edits were lost or never made.
answer: Inspect the skip-worktree and assume-unchanged bits with 'git ls-files -v | grep "^[Sh]"', where 'S' means skip-worktree and lowercase 'h' means assume-unchanged. Clear them with 'git update-index --no-skip-worktree <path>' and 'git update-index --no-assume-unchanged <path>', then re-check status. Verify by confirming the diff reappears and by deciding whether the local change should live in an ignored override file instead of a tracked one.

instruction: Your bisect run script passes on some revisions and fails on others inconsistently, and the flaky test corrupts the result. Explain how to make the search valid.
reasoning: Bisect assumes the predicate is deterministic, so a flaky check can mark a good revision bad and discard an entire half of the search space. The fix is to strengthen the predicate before continuing, not to average results afterwards. A fast, precise reproduction beats a broad unreliable one.
answer: Replace the flaky suite with a narrow reproduction that exercises only the suspected behaviour, run each revision several times to measure variance, and only then resume with 'git bisect run'. Where flakiness cannot be eliminated, bisect on a stronger signal such as an assertion count or a specific error string, and re-verify the candidate commit manually at the end. Verify by confirming the identified commit reproduces the failure deterministically and its parent does not.

instruction: 'git status' says clean but you just edited a file inside a nested directory that contains its own .git folder. Explain what you are looking at and how to confirm it.
reasoning: A nested repository is a separate object store, so the outer repository sees only a pointer and reports no change when its own files are untouched. Editing inside it affects a different repository whose status you must query separately. Assuming one status covers both is how an agent believes a change is committed when it is not.
answer: Confirm the nesting with 'ls -d */.git' or 'git status --ignored' in the outer repository and check 'git submodule status' if it is a registered submodule. Then run 'git status' and 'git log -1' inside that directory to see its own state and remote. If it is a real submodule, commit there first and then record the new pointer in the parent with 'git add'. Verify by confirming the parent shows a modified submodule entry after the inner commit.

instruction: You need to discard all changes to 'src/router.ts' including staged ones. Compare 'git checkout -- path', 'git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree path' and 'git reset HEAD path' followed by a restore, and choose safely.
reasoning: These commands operate on different areas, index versus working tree, and using one where two are needed leaves a half-restored file. The operation is destructive, so stating the desired end state before acting and confirming it afterwards is what makes it safe. Precision prevents both residual changes and lost unrelated work.
answer: Prefer 'git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree src/router.ts', which resets both areas explicitly, or the two-step 'git reset HEAD -- path' then 'git restore path'. Note that 'git checkout -- path' restores only the working tree from the index, so staged content would remain. Before discarding, check whether any part is worth keeping with 'git diff HEAD -- path', since unstaged work is unrecoverable. Verify with 'git status' and 'git diff HEAD -- path' both empty.

instruction: You want the history of a specific function in a large file, not the file's history. Explain which git command narrows to a line range and the caveat about how it tracks code.
reasoning: File-level logs bury the change you care about, while a line-range log filters to commits that touched those lines. The caveat is that the range is positional, so unrelated edits that shift lines can produce a misleading list. Knowing the mechanism bounds your confidence.
answer: Use 'git log -L :functionName:src/pricing.ts' when the function name is resolvable, or 'git log -L 120,180:src/pricing.ts' for a line range, and follow with 'git show <sha>' on the candidates to read the actual edits. Verify that the reported commits still describe the same code region by checking each diff, since positions move. For renames, add '--follow' where supported and confirm with 'git log --follow --oneline -- <path>'.

instruction: The deploy log says the release is 'production' but you cannot find your commit in it. Explain the git checks that settle whether the deploy contained your work and why the branch name is not evidence.
reasoning: A deploy may have built an earlier snapshot of the branch, or a different branch entirely, so the label describes intent rather than content. Ancestry tests answer whether a commit is included regardless of what the ref is called. The question is about the commit graph.
answer: Fetch, then test with 'git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-sha> origin/production' and list what the branch contains with 'git log --oneline -10 origin/production'. If absent, check whether the pipeline built a tagged release instead, using 'git tag --contains <your-sha>', and compare the deployed artifact's embedded version or build metadata. Verify by reading the deploy job's recorded commit from the CI run rather than inferring it from names.

instruction: You need to stash only the changes to 'src/server.ts' while leaving three other modified files untouched. Explain how and what to verify before and after.
reasoning: A whole-tree stash would remove work you intend to keep, and the resulting absence looks like a bug in the other files. Path-limited stashing exists precisely for this, but the stash entry can be ambiguous later, so a message and a verification of what remains are part of the operation. Selective state management needs explicit confirmation.
answer: Run 'git stash push -m "server wip" -- src/server.ts', then confirm the other three files still show as modified with 'git status' and that the target file matches HEAD. Inspect the entry later with 'git stash show -p stash@{0}' before applying, since a path-limited stash still records only part of the tree. Verify by re-running the search for your edit in the stashed file to confirm it is gone and that no unintended file was included.

instruction: You committed to a feature branch and pushed, but the pull request shows no new commit. Explain the diagnostics that locate where the commit actually went.
reasoning: The commit exists locally regardless of what the remote shows, so the question is which ref was pushed and to which remote, not whether the work was saved. Upstream tracking, remote names and branch renaming are frequent causes. Reading refs answers it in seconds.
answer: Confirm the commit is local with 'git log --oneline -3', then check what you pushed with 'git rev-parse HEAD' versus 'git rev-parse @{u}' and the upstream name with 'git rev-parse --abbrev-ref @{u}', which reveals a mismatch such as pushing to a fork remote or a differently named branch. Inspect remotes with 'git remote -v' and verify with 'git ls-remote origin refs/heads/<branch>' to read the remote's actual tip. Verify the fix by re-pushing to the intended ref and confirming the PR updates.

instruction: A merge you performed locally is wrong and already pushed to a shared branch. Explain the fix-forward options and why 'revert the merge' has a subtlety that a normal revert does not.
reasoning: Reverting a merge commit requires naming its parent, because a merge has two. Reverting the merge does not undo changes later merged into that branch. A plain revert of an ordinary commit has no such choice. The subtlety is the source of the classic 'reverted revert restores the bad code' problem.
answer: Revert with 'git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>', which keeps the first parent and undoes the merged branch's effect, and be aware that re-merging that branch later will not reintroduce the changes unless you revert the revert or rebase the branch to create new commits. Alternatively fix forward with a corrective commit if only part of the merge was bad. Verify by diffing the branch against its pre-merge state, 'git diff <pre-merge> HEAD --stat', and by re-running the tests that the bad merge broke.

instruction: node_modules was committed by accident in an early commit and you want it out of future work. Explain what version control can and cannot undo, and the sensible scope of a fix.
reasoning: Removing files from the index and ignoring them prevents future commits, but history retains the blobs, so clone size and any secrets inside stay exposed. Rewriting history is possible but rewrites shared commits. The right scope depends on whether the content is merely large or actually sensitive.
answer: Run 'git rm -r --cached node_modules' so local files stay on disk, add the ignore rule, and verify with 'git check-ignore -v node_modules/<pkg>'. If credentials were included, rotate them, since removal does not unpublish content. Consider history rewriting, for example with filter-repo, only with team agreement, because it invalidates every clone and open branch. Verify by checking 'git count-objects -vH' before and after any rewrite and confirming a fresh clone no longer fetches the packages.

instruction: You need to know whether a bug exists on the branch that production deploys from, without checking it out and while carrying dirty files. Explain the read-only inspection sequence.
reasoning: Read-only queries against revisions answer the question without touching the working tree, which matters when uncommitted work could be lost or when a watcher would react to file changes. Checking out for diagnosis is a side effect many agents overlook. Choosing a non-mutating tool is a safety decision.
answer: Compare revisions directly: 'git diff --stat HEAD origin/production -- src/relevant' to see divergence, and read the deployed branch's file with 'git show origin/production:src/relevant.ts'. Test membership of the suspected fix with 'git tag --contains <sha>' or 'git branch -r --contains <sha>'. Verify by reproducing against that revision in a scratch worktree if execution is required, leaving the current tree and its running server untouched.

instruction: Two branches both modified the same migration file, and the merge resolved with one side. Explain how to verify the resolution did not lose a schema change.
reasoning: A resolution that takes one side is syntactically valid and semantically incomplete, which is the dangerous class of merge error. The check must compare content across all three revisions rather than trust the absence of conflict markers. Migration files define state transitions, so losing one silently corrupts the schema.
answer: Diff the resolved file against each parent with 'git diff HEAD^1 HEAD -- migrations' and 'git diff HEAD^2 HEAD -- migrations' to see exactly what was dropped, and confirm both changes are represented, since two migrations adding different columns must both survive. Then compare the schema your ORM declares against a fresh database built from the merged migrations. Verify by resetting a scratch database and confirming 'migration status' shows both applied and the resulting schema matches.

instruction: A 'git status' after your commit shows the commit as empty and the changes still present. Explain two mechanisms that produce this and the checks that distinguish them.
reasoning: An apparently empty commit usually means the changes were never staged, or were staged in a different repository than the one being inspected, both of which look like a git failure from the inside. The distinction is found by reading the index and the repository root rather than retrying. Recognising that status output is relative to a chosen repository is the general skill.
answer: Check the staged state with 'git diff --cached --stat'; if it is empty, the changes were never added. Confirm which repository you are in with 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel' and 'git status --porcelain=v1' to see whether the paths match your expectation, since an outer or nested repository changes what is tracked. Verify by staging, re-checking 'git diff --cached', committing, and confirming 'git show --stat HEAD' lists the files.

instruction: The repository contains 'package-lock.json', 'pnpm-lock.yaml' and an '.npmrc', and the README says 'npm install'. Determine the actual package manager and the evidence hierarchy you would use.
reasoning: Lockfiles indicate what the team's installs produced, while documentation drifts, and a stale lockfile from an abandoned migration is common. The strongest evidence is what CI runs, because that pipeline is exercised continuously. Choosing a manager by file presence alone risks regenerating the wrong artifact.
answer: Check the CI workflow and any 'packageManager' field in package.json, which pins the manager and version used by the toolchain, then compare lockfile modification times with 'git log -1 --format=%ci -- package-lock.json pnpm-lock.yaml'; the more recently updated file reflects current practice. Confirm from '.npmrc' settings whether one manager is configured exclusively. Use the manager CI uses and do not create or update the other lockfile. Verify by running the same install command as CI and confirming no lockfile churn in 'git status'.

instruction: A build fails with 'Cannot find module react' although it is installed, and the project uses pnpm while the fix was written for npm. Explain the layout difference that produces this and two legitimate resolutions.
reasoning: npm's hoisted tree makes transitive packages incidentally importable, whereas pnpm's symlinked store exposes only declared dependencies. So code that relies on an undeclared import works under one manager and not the other. The failure is a missing declaration, not a broken install. Recognising the layout explains the discrepancy without reinstalling.
answer: Declare the missing dependency explicitly in the package that imports it, which is correct under both managers, or as a last resort configure public hoisting, for example a 'shamefully-hoist' or 'public-hoist-pattern' setting in .npmrc, which restores npm-like behaviour at the cost of hiding the problem. Verify by running the build with a fresh, isolated install, and check whether other undeclared imports exist by grepping for imports of packages absent from package.json.

instruction: CI fails with 'npm ci can only install with an existing package-lock.json ... lock file does not satisfy'. Explain the meaning of that message and the correct repair, as opposed to running 'npm install' and committing.
reasoning: The lockfile is a promise about resolution, and ci enforces it, so a mismatch means the manifest and lockfile were committed out of sync. Regenerating silently with a plain install is fine, but committing whatever it happens to resolve can pull unrelated upgrades. The repair must be minimal and explainable.
answer: Reconcile deliberately: update only the affected entry, for example 'npm install <pkg>@<version>', then inspect 'git diff package-lock.json' to confirm the change is limited to that package and its dependents. If the diff is huge, someone edited package.json without reinstalling, so regenerate and review whether other upgrades are acceptable, ideally in a separate commit. Verify by running 'npm ci' locally, which must succeed cleanly, and by confirming CI passes without additional version changes.

instruction: 'npm install' fails with ERESOLVE explaining a peer conflict, and a teammate suggests adding '--legacy-peer-deps'. Explain what that flag actually changes and how to decide whether it is appropriate.
reasoning: The flag relaxes resolution rather than fixing compatibility, so it can install a tree that the peer dependency contract says is unsupported. Whether that is safe depends on the specific conflict and the ecosystem's actual compatibility. Treating it as a generic repair hides real breakage behind a green install.
answer: Read the reported requirement chain to identify which package demands which peer range, then check the packages' documentation for supported versions. Prefer aligning versions so resolution succeeds without the flag, or override a single range if the upstream package is simply conservative. Use '--legacy-peer-deps' only with a recorded justification, and note that '--force' is worse because it overrides more. Verify by running the test suite and by confirming 'npm ls' reports no unmet peers.

instruction: CI runs 'npm ci', prints 'up to date' after an install, and yet a module is missing at runtime. Explain what 'up to date' does and does not mean here.
reasoning: The tool compares declared ranges with what it finds in node_modules and reports no action needed, which is not a verification that the tree matches the lockfile or that files exist on disk. Partial or corrupted installs satisfy a version check while missing contents. A no-op message is not a health report.
answer: Verify the artifact rather than the message: check the package's presence and integrity with 'ls node_modules/<pkg>/package.json' and compare the version with the lockfile entry, then run a clean 'npm ci' which deletes and rebuilds the tree from the lockfile, unlike 'npm install'. If a platform-specific or optional dependency is absent, check whether the install ran with '--omit=optional' or an unsupported CPU. Verify by resolving the module from Node and confirming the path it reports.

instruction: After a teammate ran an install, the lockfile diff shows 900 changed packages although only one dependency version was intended. Explain the two most likely causes and how you would decide whether to accept the diff.
reasoning: A large diff can come from an unrelated manager or lockfile-version upgrade, which rewrites formatting without changing resolutions, or from real dependency drift because someone edited the manifest without a scoped install. The remedies are opposite: one is safe to accept, the other needs review. Attribution is the decision.
answer: First check the 'lockfileVersion' field in the before and after diff; a bump means a different tool version rewrote the file, so either align versions using the 'packageManager' field or revert and re-run with the expected manager. Then list the actual version changes with 'git diff -- package-lock.json | rg "^[-+]\s+\"version\""' to see how many packages genuinely moved. Accept only changes you can attribute to the intended dependency, and if not, regenerate the lockfile from the base revision with a scoped install. Verify with 'npm ls' and a clean install.

instruction: A monorepo uses the 'workspace:*' protocol in one package's dependencies, and npm reports it cannot resolve that range. Explain the mechanism and why this is not a broken dependency.
reasoning: Workspace protocols are understood only by managers with workspace support, and an unsupported or misconfigured manager sees an invalid semver range. The dependency is correct in intent and unresolvable in tooling, which is a mismatch rather than a mistake in package.json. Diagnosing it requires knowing which layer is failing.
answer: Confirm the manager and settings: check the root manifest for a 'workspaces' array or a pnpm-workspace file, since npm and yarn resolve workspace links only when the packages are declared, and the 'workspace:' prefix is a pnpm and yarn convention that npm's older versions reject. Use the manager the repository specifies, and install from the root so the workspace graph is visible. Verify by confirming the local package is symlinked rather than fetched from the registry.

instruction: The Dockerfile builds with 'ENV NODE_ENV=production' before 'npm ci', and the build then fails because the bundler is missing. Explain the interaction and where the flag should be set.
reasoning: The environment variable changes install behaviour, not just runtime mode, because the package manager omits devDependencies when it is set during installation. A build tool is a devDependency, so a production install cannot compile. The ordering of environment setup relative to install is the whole problem.
answer: Move 'ENV NODE_ENV=production' after the build steps, or install with an explicit flag such as '--include=dev' for the build stage and produce a production tree in a later stage, which is the usual multi-stage pattern. Confirm by reading which packages the failing stage needs versus what the install log reports installing. Verify by rebuilding and confirming both the bundler is present during the build and the final image omits dev dependencies.

instruction: 'npm install' succeeds but prints three 'npm WARN EBADENGINE' lines naming a Node version requirement. Explain how to determine whether this is fatal and what to verify before running the app.
reasoning: The manager warns and continues by default, so a successful exit does not mean the declared requirement was met; whether the code then works is unknown. Engines are advisory unless strictness is configured. The distinction between a warning and a constraint depends on configuration you must check.
answer: Check whether strict enforcement is on with 'npm config get engine-strict' and look for an '.npmrc' setting, then compare the required range with the active version from 'node -v' and with the repository's pinned version in .nvmrc, engines, and the Dockerfile. Run the app or its tests to see whether the mismatch is actually observable. Verify by switching to a compliant Node version, for example via the version manager, and confirming both the warnings and any runtime failure disappear.

instruction: You must install a package from a git URL for a temporary fix. Explain what the lockfile will record and why that has consequences for reproducibility and for the eventual removal.
reasoning: Git-sourced dependencies pin a commit and are fetched over a protocol that requires credentials and network access at install time, unlike registry tarballs. This can break CI for others and makes the dependency effectively unversioned by semver. The temporary state has to be planned for removal at install time.
answer: After installing, inspect the resolved entry, which records a URL with a commit hash, and confirm CI can authenticate to that host or the install will fail for everyone. Prefer a published version, a registry tarball, or a committed patch approach if the change is small, and open a follow-up to replace the pin once upstream releases. Verify by running a clean install in an environment without your git credentials, which is the realistic test of whether the dependency is portable.

instruction: 'npm audit' reports 42 vulnerabilities but 'npm audit fix' would introduce a major version bump for a core framework. Explain how to triage rather than blindly fix.
reasoning: Advisory counts conflate reachability, severity and fixability, and an automatic fix that upgrades a major framework version can break working code while closing an advisory that never applied to you. Security output is evidence requiring interpretation, not a task list. The goal is risk reduction, not a zero count.
answer: Inspect the paths with 'npm ls <package>' to see whether the vulnerable version is reachable from production code or only from a development tool, and check whether the affected function is used at all, since some advisories are conditionally exploitable. Read the advisory's patched range and the framework's breaking changes before deciding, then fix directly-attributable issues and, where a transitive package cannot be upgraded, record an override with justification. Verify by re-running audit and confirming that remaining items are documented as accepted risk, and run the full test suite after any upgrade.

instruction: A lockfile conflict appears during a rebase. Explain the safe resolution and why hand-editing the merged region usually fails.
reasoning: A lockfile is a resolved graph with integrity hashes, so stitching together textual halves produces an internally inconsistent document that may install or may not, and the failure surfaces later in CI. The file is derived data, and derived data is regenerated rather than merged by hand. Knowing this changes the whole approach.
answer: Take one side's lockfile and regenerate the resolutions with the manager, for example 'git checkout --theirs package-lock.json' then 'npm install', so the resolver recomputes the graph for the merged manifest, or use a merge driver configured for the lockfile if the repository provides one. Confirm 'git diff' afterwards shows only the intended additions. Verify with 'npm ci' that the manifest and lockfile agree, and run the tests, because a syntactically valid lockfile can still resolve a version incompatible with the merged code.

instruction: Two lockfiles exist at the repository root, 'package-lock.json' and 'yarn.lock', with different resolved versions for the same package. Explain which to trust for a running build and how to prove it.
reasoning: The lockfile that the pipeline actually consumes defines the build, and a second one is usually a migration residue that nothing reads. Trusting the more recently modified file is a guess. Provenance comes from the commands the CI executes and the manager pinned in the manifest.
answer: Read the CI workflow and Dockerfile install commands to see which manager is invoked, and check the 'packageManager' field for a pin. Confirm the effective version by resolving the installed module's version in the environment where the build runs, which is the only authority for what executed. Treat the other lockfile as stale and propose removing it, since dual lockfiles cause divergent installs across contributors. Verify by running the CI install command locally and confirming no lockfile churn.

instruction: After upgrading a package from v3 to v4, the module resolves at runtime but importing a subpath throws 'PACKAGE_SUBPATH_NOT_FOUND'. Explain the manifest field responsible and how to verify what is allowed.
reasoning: An exports map restricts which internal paths consumers may import, replacing the previous behaviour where any file was reachable, so an upgrade can remove access without changing the main entry. Reading the field, not guessing from the file tree, establishes the permitted surface. A resolved main import is not evidence that deep imports still work.
answer: Open the dependency's package.json and read its 'exports' field to see the allowed subpaths and conditions, and check the release notes for the removal of the path you used. Switch to a documented entry point, or request the missing export upstream. Verify with 'node -e "console.log(require.resolve(\"pkg/sub\"))"', which reproduces the failure, and re-test after choosing a supported specifier so the fix is observed rather than assumed.

instruction: 'npm install' on a Linux CI runner fails with 'ENOTEMPTY: directory not empty, rename', while it works locally. Explain the likely mechanism and the recovery.
reasoning: This error typically follows an interrupted write, a stale node_modules with files the current platform cannot remove, or a concurrent install sharing a cache, so it is an environment-state problem rather than a dependency problem. Repeating the same command usually reproduces it. Recovery means removing the corrupted state deliberately.
answer: Check for a leftover partial rename, for example a temporary directory inside node_modules, and for a concurrent process holding files with 'lsof +D node_modules'. Confirm the layer state in the image and whether the cache is shared, then repair deterministically with 'rm -rf node_modules && npm cache verify && npm ci' so the tree is rebuilt from the lockfile. Verify by re-running in CI once, and if the error recurs on the runner, investigate filesystem or volume sharing rather than the dependency set.

instruction: CI sets 'ignore-scripts=true' in '.npmrc' and the build then fails because a native module is unbuilt. Explain the trade-off recorded by that setting and how to fix it without disabling the protection entirely.
reasoning: Disabling lifecycle scripts is a supply-chain defence that also suppresses legitimate install-time builds, so the failure is the intended side effect of a security choice. Blindly removing the setting quietly reverses a deliberate decision. The correct fix re-enables building narrowly.
answer: Keep scripts blocked by default and allow only the packages that genuinely need them, using an allow-list mechanism if the manager supports it, or move native compilation into an explicit build step you control. Check the image for prebuilt binaries, since many native packages ship platform-specific optional dependencies that need no script at all. Verify by confirming the module loads with 'node -p "require(\"pkg\").version"' and that the ignore setting is still present in the configuration.

instruction: A private package returns '404 Not Found' during install in CI but installs locally, and no error mentions authentication. Explain why 404 is the expected unauthenticated response and how to verify.
reasoning: Private registries deliberately return not-found rather than unauthorised to avoid confirming a package's existence, so a missing token presents as a 404. Reading it as a typo in the package name sends the investigation to package.json instead of to credentials. The status code encodes a policy, not a fact.
answer: Check the registry configuration the process actually uses, from the project's and user's '.npmrc' and any 'npm config get registry' in that environment, and confirm the CI secret is present without printing it, for example 'printenv NPM_TOKEN | wc -c'. Test resolution of the metadata endpoint with a request that includes the auth header and inspect the status. Verify by installing again in a clean container that mimics CI, not in your authenticated local shell.

instruction: A fresh checkout runs 'npm install' successfully, then 'npm ls' prints 'UNMET PEER DEPENDENCY'. Explain whether this proves the app is broken and what to inspect next.
reasoning: Peer metadata describes declared compatibility, and an unmet peer is a warning about a contract, not an observed failure; conversely, its absence does not prove the code works. The next step is to test the behaviour the peer relationship governs, such as a shared singleton or context. Treating warnings as verdicts goes both ways.
answer: Read the chain with 'npm ls <peer-package> --all' to see which consumers expect which range, and check whether two copies of the peer were installed, which is a real failure mode for context- and instance-sensitive libraries. Then exercise the feature that depends on it in a test or a manual request. Verify by aligning versions so 'npm ls' reports no unmet peers and confirming the behaviour test still passes, which ties the warning to observed evidence.

instruction: 'npm outdated' reports a package is out of date, but the lockfile pins a newer version than package.json allows. Explain how both statements can be true and which describes the installed code.
reasoning: The outdated command compares the manifest's range with the registry's latest release, while the lockfile records what is installed, and both can be correct about different things. Neither, however, is proof about the runtime, where a nested duplicate may differ. Confusing declared, resolved and loaded versions is the trap.
answer: Compare all three layers deliberately: the range in package.json, the resolved version in the lockfile, and the version actually installed, which you obtain by resolving the module and reading its package.json from the installed tree. Check for duplicates with 'npm ls <pkg> --all'. Verify by deciding which version you intend, aligning the manifest range, reinstalling, and confirming the installed version matches the lockfile entry.

instruction: You must upgrade React from 17 to 18 in a large application. Explain the sequence of inspection that should precede editing package.json, and the verification that the upgrade is actually complete.
reasoning: A major upgrade touches transitive peers, type definitions and deprecated APIs, so editing one line and hoping is not a plan. The evidence needed is what else depends on the current major version and which breaking changes affect this codebase. Completion means the whole graph agrees, not that the app renders once.
answer: Before editing, list dependents with 'npm ls react --all', read the migration guide for breaking changes, and check whether ecosystem packages support the new major, for example the router, state libraries and test utilities. Then upgrade, resolve peer conflicts by updating dependents rather than forcing, and run the type check plus the full test suite, since deprecated APIs often fail type checking first. Verify completion by confirming only one copy of React is installed, that peer warnings are gone, and that the build and tests pass with the lockfile committed.

instruction: A Dockerfile runs 'RUN npm install' before copying source, and builds are slow even when nothing changed, sometimes pulling newer patch versions. Explain both problems and the corrected pattern.
reasoning: Layer caching is invalidated by whatever the instruction reads, so copying only manifests before install keeps the cache, while a floating install command re-resolves versions and breaks reproducibility between builds. One line explains both symptoms. The fix is to bind the install to a committed resolution.
answer: Copy package.json and the lockfile first, run 'npm ci' rather than 'npm install', then copy the source, so the dependency layer is reused until the lockfile changes. Confirm by rebuilding without edits and observing a cached layer in the build output, and by verifying the installed tree matches the lockfile. Verify also that the cache key or image layer store is not configured to bypass caching, since a cache-busting build argument can explain persistent slowness.

instruction: You must add a library used only by 'packages/admin' in a pnpm workspace. Compare installing from the root with a filter, installing inside the package directory, and editing the manifest by hand. Justify the choice.
reasoning: Workspace installs are scoped by where the command runs and by flags, and the wrong scope can add the dependency to the root manifest or fail to update the lockfile, producing a state that satisfies your machine but not CI. Manual manifest edits skip resolution entirely. Choosing the invocation that the repository supports is what keeps the graph consistent.
answer: Run the install scoped to the package, for example 'pnpm add <lib> --filter admin' from the root, or 'pnpm add <lib' inside the package, which updates that package's manifest and the shared lockfile together. Never hand-edit version ranges, because resolution and integrity data are the manager's job. Verify by confirming 'git status' shows only the package manifest and the root lockfile changed, and by running 'pnpm ls <lib> --filter admin' plus a build of that workspace.

instruction: A production container crashes with 'Cannot find module lodash', which resolves fine on your laptop. Explain the packaging distinction that accounts for it and how to confirm the classification of that dependency.
reasoning: Local installs include devDependencies while production installs omit them, so a runtime requirement declared as a dev dependency works until it reaches the deployment target. The error's presence only in production is itself evidence about declaration rather than about the environment. Confirming the field is a one-line check.
answer: Check which field lists it with 'git grep -n "lodash" -- package.json */package.json', and confirm the runtime import by finding the require or import statement. If it is a build-time helper only, fix the import instead; if it is genuinely runtime, move it to dependencies with the manager so the lockfile stays consistent. Verify by installing with '--omit=dev' in a scratch directory and confirming the module resolves, which reproduces production conditions locally.

instruction: You removed a package with 'npm uninstall' and now CI fails resolving a different package that you did not touch. Explain the mechanism and the verification that would have caught it earlier.
reasoning: Uninstalling can drop a transitive package that code was relying on through hoisting, so the failure lands somewhere unrelated to the removal. A green local run may still work by accident if the leftover tree had not been rebuilt. Verification requires an install from a clean state, not an incremental one.
answer: Inspect what changed with 'git diff -- package-lock.json' and search for imports of the removed package's transitive dependencies, for example with 'rg -n "from .<removed-pkg>"'. Reproduce the CI conditions with 'rm -rf node_modules && npm ci', which exposes reliance on hoisted packages that an incremental install hides. Verify by adding the missing dependency explicitly where it is imported, then confirming a clean install resolves it.

instruction: The CI install is fast for colleagues but takes four minutes on your branch after you edited '.npmrc'. Explain which interactions between that file and the package manager you should investigate.
reasoning: A project-level configuration file silently overrides registry, proxy, cache location and fetch behaviour for everyone using the repository, so a single line can disable a warm cache or reroute requests. The symptom is a performance change whose cause is configuration. Reading the file's effect is faster than bisecting the pipeline.
answer: Diff your '.npmrc' against the base revision and check for a changed registry, a disabled cache, an alternate cache directory that misses CI's cached path, or added strict-ssl and fetch-retry settings that alter request behaviour. Confirm by timing an install with the settings removed and comparing. Verify by restoring the previous configuration, re-running CI, and confirming the cache key and path in the workflow match what the manager writes, since a moved cache directory looks identical to a cold cache.

instruction: The install output says 'changed 3 packages' rather than 'added', and a teammate worries new code will not work. Explain how to interpret the three verbs and what to check to confirm the intended package updated.
reasoning: Package managers report tree operations, and 'changed' means a version replacement while 'added' and 'removed' describe presence. So the wording tells you about the delta shape rather than about correctness. Reading a specific verb as good or bad is a misreading. The relevant check is the resulting version.
answer: Confirm the intended package's version directly, for example 'npm ls <pkg>' and by reading the installed package's own manifest version, then compare with the lockfile entry and the range in package.json. Check 'git diff -- package-lock.json' to see which three entries moved and whether any of them is an unexpected upgrade. Verify by running the tests that depend on the new behaviour, which is the evidence that the change took effect.

instruction: On an ARM CI runner, installing the toolchain fails with a message about an optional dependency and the fallback build then breaks. Explain the mechanism and the safe remedy.
reasoning: Native packages ship per-platform binaries as optional dependencies, and a missing variant falls back to compiling from source, which needs a compiler and headers the image may not have. The failure looks like a package problem but is a platform and image problem. Optional does not mean unimportant.
answer: Read the log for which optional dependency was skipped and check whether a build of the native module started and failed, for example by looking for compiler invocations. Confirm the architecture with 'uname -m' and the Node ABI with 'node -p process.versions.modules', and either install the missing platform variant of the package or add the build tools in the image. Verify with a clean install on the same runner architecture, since reproducing on a different CPU proves nothing.

instruction: A monorepo package depends on a sibling with 'file:../shared' and behaves differently in CI than locally, with stale code from 'shared' being used. Explain the mechanism and how to verify which copy is loaded.
reasoning: A file reference may be installed as a copy or a link depending on the manager and flags. So local edits can be invisible after the first install, and CI resolves a published or copied version instead. Reading the file's contents locally says nothing about what the consumer loads. Path resolution is the evidence.
answer: Check what the installed entry is: 'ls -l node_modules/shared' shows whether it is a symlink or a real directory copy, and resolve from the consumer with 'node -e "console.log(require.resolve(\"shared\"))"'. Prefer workspace protocols over file references so linking is explicit, and reinstall after changes if a copy-based install is unavoidable. Verify by editing a marker string in 'shared' and confirming the consumer observes it in CI's environment, not only locally.

instruction: You need a transitive security fix but no release of your direct dependency includes it. Explain the manifest mechanism for forcing a resolution and the risks you must record.
reasoning: Pinning a transitive version from above overrides the resolution the dependency's own range was written for, which can install an API-incompatible version silently. The legitimate tools, overrides and resolutions, exist for exactly this case but shift responsibility to your repository. The trade-off is real and must be documented.
answer: Use the manager's override mechanism, for example an 'overrides' block in npm's package.json or 'pnpm.overrides', and never edit the lockfile entry by hand. Then confirm the resolved version with 'npm ls <pkg> --all' and check whether more than one copy remains, since multiple copies mean the fix may not apply to all code paths. Verify by running the full test suite, recording the override with a comment and a follow-up to remove it when the direct dependency releases, and note that if the package is not actually reachable in production code, an accepted-risk note may be preferable.

instruction: A teammate uses 'npm link' to develop a library against the app and reports strange runtime errors like two instances of the same framework. Explain the mechanism and the better workflow.
reasoning: A linked package brings its own dependency tree and resolves modules from its own directory. So the app and the library can load separate copies of a package that must be a singleton. The symptom, duplicated state or context errors, is a resolution artifact rather than a code bug. Workspaces exist to avoid this.
answer: Replace the link with a workspace dependency or install the library's peer into the same tree, and verify singleton status by listing copies with 'npm ls react --all' or by comparing resolved paths from the app and from the library. If linking is unavoidable, dedupe peers or configure the bundler to resolve them to one location. Verify by checking that only one copy of the shared dependency is loaded at runtime, which is the observable that distinguishes a correct setup.

instruction: The repository uses Yarn PnP and your editor reports 'cannot find module' for packages the build resolves correctly. Explain what the editor is missing and how to confirm the install is fine.
reasoning: Plug-and-play resolution has no node_modules directory, so tools that assume the classic layout cannot find packages even when the loader works. The discrepancy is about resolver configuration, not about a broken install. Distinguishing tool-level failure from project-level failure prevents a pointless reinstall.
answer: Confirm with 'yarn install --immutable' that resolution succeeds and with 'yarn why <pkg>' that the package is in the resolution, then give the editor the same view by generating the editor plugin setup with 'yarn set -d' style commands or the Yarn SDK for TypeScript and ESLint, which supply the Plug'n'Play resolution to language services. Verify by restarting the language server and confirming diagnostics match the build.

instruction: 'npm install -g' fails with EACCES on a managed machine, and the workaround proposed is 'sudo npm install -g'. Explain the risk and two safer alternatives for a CLI tool needed only by this project.
reasoning: Installing as root into a shared prefix puts user-writable package code into a location that other users' tooling may execute, and mixes global state with per-user version managers. The need is usually local, so a global install is the wrong scope. Alternatives exist that avoid both privilege and shared state.
answer: Prefer a project devDependency, then run it through 'npx --no-install <tool>', which uses the local version, or use the manager's user-scoped prefix configured under your home directory, which a version manager already provides. If the machine is managed, request the tool through the approved channel rather than escalating. Verify by confirming 'command -v <tool>' resolves to a path inside the project or your user prefix, and that CI, which uses the project install, also finds it.

instruction: The package install log shows a postinstall script failing, but the app still starts. Explain how to determine whether that failure matters, and what running the app proves about it.
reasoning: Install-time scripts often prepare native builds, generate files, or install binaries. So a failing one may leave artifacts missing that only surface on a particular code path. A successful start is weak evidence of health. Verification must exercise the affected path specifically.
answer: Read which script failed and what it produces, then check for its expected artifact, for example a built binary, a generated client, or a downloaded toolchain. Exercise the specific feature rather than the boot path, and compare a clean install against the current tree, since incremental installs skip steps. Verify by re-running the install in a scratch copy and confirming the script succeeds, or record the failure with a justification if the artifact is genuinely unused, which is a decision rather than an observation.

instruction: 'audit fix --force' proposes downgrading three packages to satisfy an advisory. Explain how to evaluate that proposal before running it, and what to check afterwards.
reasoning: The forced flag rewrites manifest ranges as needed, including downgrades that reintroduce removed features and known other vulnerabilities, and its exit status does not tell you whether the result is safe. The output is a suggestion, not a recommendation to apply. Evaluating means reading the plan first.
answer: Inspect the proposed changes with a dry run or on a branch so 'git diff -- package.json package-lock.json' shows every range rewrite, then check the downgrade targets' changelogs for breaking removals and whether the advisory actually applies to code you run. Prefer a targeted upgrade or an override for the single vulnerable path. Verify by running the full test suite and 'npm ls' to confirm no duplicate or incompatible versions, and document accepted advisories when no safe fix exists.

instruction: A dependency update PR from a bot shows only a lockfile change with no manifest diff, yet the resolved version is newer. Explain how a version can change without a manifest edit and how to review it.
reasoning: Ranges such as carets float, so a fresh install resolves a newer patch that the old lockfile pinned; the manifest is unchanged because the range already permitted it. The lockfile is therefore the real review surface. Ignoring a lockfile-only diff misses genuine code changes.
answer: Read the lockfile diff for version and integrity changes, then check the upstream release notes and compare the two tags for the released range, since a patch release can include behaviour changes. Confirm whether the PR's install is reproducible by running 'npm ci' from the new lockfile locally. Verify by running the test suite and by checking the resolved version matches what the range allows, recording any package that floated beyond its tested version.

instruction: You need to prove a fix works in the containerized production configuration, but the container runs 'npm ci --omit=dev'. Explain what local verification cannot establish and the sequence that can.
reasoning: Development installs include dev-only tooling and different resolutions, so behaviour that depends on module presence, entry points, or build-time transforms cannot be inferred from a local run. Verifying inside the target configuration is the only equivalent. Environment parity is the standard here.
answer: Build the image with your change and run the same install flags, then execute the app's real entry point inside it, resolving the module the way production will with 'node -e "console.log(require.resolve(\"pkg\"))"'. Check whether anything the runtime needs is declared as a devDependency. Verify by comparing the installed tree's package count and versions with the intended lockfile, and by running a smoke request against the container rather than trusting that the local app worked.

instruction: 'npm ci' unexpectedly deletes and rebuilds the whole tree, and a teammate complains that their manually patched package inside node_modules vanished. Explain the design intent and the correct fix.
reasoning: The command exists to produce a tree exactly matching the lockfile, so removing and recreating node_modules is a guarantee rather than a side effect. Anything not recorded in the manifest or lockfile is therefore not reproducible. The conflict is with hand edits, not with the tool.
answer: Explain that a hand patch in node_modules is invisible to every other environment, so it was never a fix. Record the change as a patch file applied by the toolchain, for example patch-package for npm or a patchedDependencies entry for pnpm, or fork the dependency if the change is substantial. Verify by running 'npm ci' again and confirming the patched behaviour survives, and check that CI runs the patch step, since a postinstall that is skipped by a no-scripts setting would silently lose the fix.

instruction: Installing a package with 'npm install pkg@latest' on a project whose lockfile is version 1 while your npm writes version 3 produces a huge diff. Explain the cause and the least-disruptive path.
reasoning: The lockfile format belongs to the manager version, so an upgrade rewrites the whole file and buries the real change in format noise, which reviewers then cannot audit. The intended dependency change is a one-line delta inside a regenerated document. Choosing the format is a team decision, not an install detail.
answer: Check the 'packageManager' field or CI to see the expected manager version, and either use that version for the install, for example through the Node version manager's bundled npm, or accept the format change as a separate, clearly labelled commit. Verify the semantic delta by extracting only version and integrity lines from the diff rather than reading it whole. Confirm the install still works with the CI command, since a newer format may be unreadable by an older pinned manager.

instruction: You added a dependency and the install succeeded, but the next developer's 'npm ci' fails with a missing integrity. Explain what state you committed and how to check that both files are consistent before pushing.
reasoning: The manifest declares a requirement while the lockfile records the resolution and its integrity. So committing one without the other produces a tree that installs for the author and fails everywhere else. The mismatch is invisible locally because your node_modules already satisfies it. Verification requires the clean-install path, not an incremental install.
answer: Inspect 'git status' for an uncommitted lockfile and confirm with 'git diff --stat' which files the change touched. Regenerate both together with the manager's install command, then verify consistency by running 'npm ci' in a scratch copy or after deleting node_modules, which is the exact operation that fails for others. Check that the lockfile is not ignored, since 'git check-ignore package-lock.json' returning true explains why it was never committed.

instruction: A teammate reports the app installs different dependency versions on two days with no code change. Explain which practice makes that possible and the command that reproduces the intended tree deterministically.
reasoning: Without a committed resolution, installs resolve floating ranges at execution time. So upstream releases silently change your tree, which is why reproducibility depends on the lockfile rather than on the manifest. A one-off difference is evidence about the missing artifact, not about the registry. Determinism is the property being tested.
answer: Check whether a lockfile is committed with 'git ls-files | rg "lock"' and confirm 'npm ci' is what CI runs, since ci installs from the lockfile while install re-resolves. Commit the lockfile if absent, and pin the manager version too, because a differing manager can resolve differently. Verify by running the install twice on different days or in a clean container and comparing resolved versions, for example with a checksum of the 'npm ls --json' output.

instruction: Installing a package that uses node-gyp fails with 'make: command not found' inside a Debian slim image. Explain the distinction between the package being broken and the image lacking a toolchain, and the appropriate fix.
reasoning: The error names a missing system program, not a defect in the dependency, so the repair belongs in the image's build stage rather than in the manifest. Distinguishing application-level from environment-level failure prevents pointless version changes. The compiler is a build-time need, not a runtime one.
answer: Install the build tools in the stage that compiles, for example 'apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 make g++', and prefer to avoid compilation entirely by using a prebuilt variant of the dependency where one exists. Confirm which native modules need building by reading the failing package's scripts. Verify by rebuilding from a clean image state and confirming the install completes, then keep the final image free of compilers so the artifact stays small.

instruction: A dependency's postinstall downloads a headless browser, and the CI log shows a network failure to a binary host while the package manager reports success afterwards. Explain why the apparent success is misleading and what to check.
reasoning: Lifecycle scripts and package resolution are separate stages, so a package can install while its optional binary download fails or is skipped, leaving the runtime feature broken. A green install line does not verify downloaded artifacts. The claim to test is whether the binary exists where the code expects it.
answer: Verify the artifact rather than the log: check the expected browser cache path and run the library's own diagnostic, for example asking it to launch and reading the error, or checking the installed binary's version. Configure the download host or mirror for the CI network, or preinstall the browser in the image and set the environment variable that points the library at it. Verify by running one real navigation in CI, since launching is the operation the missing download affects.

instruction: The Postgres client library installs and imports fine, yet the app fails at runtime with an error mentioning a missing 'libpq' shared object on Alpine. Explain the driver-versus-library distinction and how to diagnose it.
reasoning: Some packages bundle a native component while others link against a system library that the package manager does not install. So a successful JavaScript install can coexist with an unresolvable dynamic dependency. The error is a loader complaint, not a module resolution failure. Diagnosing it means inspecting dynamic links.
answer: Inspect the compiled artifact with 'ldd' on the addon or shared object to see which library is unresolved, and compare the C library the image provides with the binary's expectation, since prebuilt packages compiled for glibc generally fail on musl. Install the system library in the image, or switch to a pure implementation or a musl-compatible build. Verify by re-running 'ldd' to confirm no missing entries and then connecting from the app, rather than treating a successful import as proof.

instruction: Rendering screenshots in a fresh container produces boxes instead of letters while the same code is correct on a laptop. Explain the missing dependency class and how to verify it without changing application code.
reasoning: Text shaping depends on system fonts and configuration libraries that are absent from minimal images, so the difference is in the base image rather than in the dependency list. No package manager error occurs, which is why it is easily misattributed. Verification is about the host environment's contents.
answer: Check what the container has with a font listing tool such as 'fc-list', and compare with the host; install the required font package and, if rendering differs by shaping, the text-shaping libraries too. Confirm the locale is configured, since missing locale data changes case folding and sorting. Verify by regenerating a screenshot in the container and diffing it against the expected output rather than trusting that the fonts installed without error.

instruction: A Python service works in your terminal but 'ModuleNotFoundError' appears when run by a systemd unit, although pip reported the package installed. Explain the interpreter-mismatch hypothesis and the checks that confirm it.
reasoning: A package installed into one interpreter or virtual environment is invisible to another. So a service running as a different user with a different executable can resolve site-packages elsewhere. That installation message describes only the interpreter your command used. The service's runtime is a separate context, and the interpreter it launches is the first thing to compare.
answer: Compare interpreters: print the executable and resolution path in both contexts, for example 'which python3' versus the unit's ExecStart path, and inside the service 'sys.executable' and 'sys.path'. Check whether the unit's user can read the virtual environment and whether an activation or absolute interpreter path is missing from the service definition. Verify by running the service's exact command as its user with the same interpreter and confirming the import succeeds.

instruction: You install a package with 'pip install -r requirements.txt' and later 'pip list' shows it, but the application imports a different version. Explain the environment inspection you need before changing versions.
reasoning: Multiple interpreters, virtual environments and user site directories can each hold a copy, so a listing from one tells you nothing about another. The import path is the only evidence about what executes. Version churn without this check just moves the problem.
answer: From inside the running application, print the module's file path and version, which shows exactly which copy is loaded, and compare with the environment your shell is using by checking the active prefix with 'python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"'. Confirm the process's environment variables for path overrides. Verify the fix by re-running the application's own probe after aligning environments, not by re-running pip.

instruction: The CI script calls 'jest' directly and fails with 'command not found', although the install step reported adding devDependencies. Explain what is on PATH and the portable way to invoke a project tool.
reasoning: Executables installed as dependencies live in the project's bin directory, which is only on PATH inside scripts run by the package manager, not in a bare shell. The install succeeded; the invocation assumed a global command. Choosing the right entry point is the fix.
answer: Invoke it through the project, for example 'npx --no-install jest' or the package manager's script runner, which prepends the local bin directory, or call the relative path directly. Confirm presence with 'ls node_modules/.bin' and that the version matches the devDependency. Verify by running the same command CI runs after deleting node_modules and reinstalling, which proves the invocation works from a clean state rather than relying on your shell's globals.

instruction: Behind a corporate proxy, installing a package fails with an error about a self-signed certificate in the chain, while 'npm config get registry' shows the internal mirror. Explain the mechanism and the fix that does not disable verification.
reasoning: TLS interception replaces the certificate with one issued by an internal authority that the runtime does not trust, so the failure is a trust-store gap rather than a network outage. Disabling verification removes a security control and hides the real requirement. The correct fix supplies the authority to the clients that need it.
answer: Add the corporate certificate authority to the trust stores used by each client: the package manager's cafile setting, the system store for git-based fetches, and the runtime's node extra-ca-certificates variable if a postinstall performs its own downloads. Verify by fetching the same URL with a request that uses the CA file and confirming success, and never set the flag that ignores certificate errors, since it silently weakens every later install.

instruction: An install was interrupted by a disk-full error and now the app fails with a syntax error inside a dependency's file. Explain the causal chain and the recovery, and why retrying the install alone may not work.
reasoning: A write that stops mid-file leaves truncated content that installs may consider present, and package managers can skip re-downloading files that appear installed. The dependency's syntax error is therefore a corruption artifact, not a bug. Recovery requires removing the state, not repeating the operation.
answer: Confirm the mechanism by checking free space with 'df -h' and inspecting the truncated file's size against the published package, then free space or move caches before reinstalling. Repair deterministically by deleting node_modules and the cache for that package and running a clean install from the lockfile, which rewrites the tree rather than assuming it is intact. Verify by re-running the previously failing import and checking the file parses, and by confirming the disk no longer fills during install.

instruction: A package requires a peer of 'ffmpeg' and works locally because you installed it manually, but CI fails with 'spawn ffmpeg ENOENT'. Explain what kind of dependency this is and how to make CI correct without relying on a global install.
reasoning: An external program invoked as a subprocess is not a package dependency at all. So the manifest cannot express it and installation of the JavaScript package will never satisfy it. Local manual setup hides the gap. The fix is to declare the requirement in the environment that runs it.
answer: Install the program in the CI image with the system package manager, or use a package that bundles a binary for the target platform, and verify the invocation path by checking the version the code executes. Confirm how the code locates the program, since an override variable or a configurable path may be the intended mechanism. Verify by running the exact failing job in a container built from the updated image, which proves the requirement is met in CI and not only on your machine.
